articles.title: MABUX: Bunker prices remain volatile in November
articles.summary: According to Sergey Ivanov, Director, MABUX, October’s global bunker market remained under strong geopolitical and supply-side pressure. Middle East tensions, disruptions to oil product flows, tight regional fuel availability and rising LNG prices continued to support bunker quotations. The key market drivers...
articles.body: According to Sergey Ivanov, Director, MABUX, October’s global bunker market remained under strong geopolitical and supply-side pressure. Middle East tensions, disruptions to oil product flows, tight regional fuel availability and rising LNG prices continued to support bunker quotations. The key market drivers included: Middle East Conflict: Continued instability around the Strait of Hormuz sustained elevated geopolitical risk premiums, freight costs and bunker price volatility. Crude Oil Supply Constraints: Disrupted Gulf oil exports, limited supply flexibility and higher transportation costs maintained upward pressure on crude and marine fuel prices. Tight Distillate Supply: Restricted gasoil availability and strong refinery margins continued to support MGO LS prices, widening premiums over residual bunker fuels. Regional Fuel Imbalances: Limited HSFO and VLSFO availability, particularly in Asian bunkering hubs, contributed to significant regional price differentials and changes in scrubber spreads. Higher Bunker Transportation Costs: Elevated tanker freight rates constrained fuel arbitrage flows between Europe and Asia, increasing supply pressure in major bunkering hubs. Rising LNG Prices: Tight global LNG supply, stronger European gas prices and seasonal demand expectations reduced LNG’s competitiveness against conventional marine fuels. Alternative Fuel Transition: Continued expansion of dual-fuel and battery-powered fleets supported the longer-term diversification of marine fuel demand, although high alternative fuel costs remained a constraint. Ivanov noted that in October, the MABUX 380 HSFO Index extended its upward trend, gaining USD 76.75, from USD 701.67/MT at the end of September to USD 778.42/MT. The VLSFO Index rose by USD 70.81, reaching USD 913.07/MT compared to USD 842.26/MT a month earlier, breaking above the USD 900/MT threshold. Meanwhile, the MGO LS Index recorded only a marginal increase of USD 2.62, edging up from USD 1,521.88/MT at the end of September to USD 1,524.50/MT. The upward trend in bunker prices during October was primarily driven by the continued escalation of the military conflict between the United States and Iran, which sustained a substantial geopolitical risk premium in global crude oil and refined petroleum product prices. At the time of reporting, MABUX bunker indices remained close to their peak levels, reflecting persistent geopolitical tensions and elevated uncertainty across global energy markets. According to Ivanov, the MABUX Global Scrubber Spread (SS) – the price differential between 380 HSFO and VLSFO – continued its moderate downward trend in October, declining by USD 5.94, from USD 140.59 at the end of September to USD 134.65, while remaining above the USD 100.00 SS Benchmark. The monthly average SS value also decreased by USD 23.78. In Rotterdam, the SS Spread increased by USD 11.00, from USD 57.00 at the end of September to USD 68.00, remaining below the USD 100.00 threshold. However, the monthly average SS value declined by USD 25.63. In Singapore, the 380 HSFO/VLSFO price differential narrowed by USD 35.00, from USD 125.00 in September to USD 90.00, falling below the USD 100.00 benchmark and briefly dropping to as low as USD 20.00 during the month. The port’s monthly average SS value also recorded a substantial decline of USD 80.33. The continued narrowing of the SS Spread suggests that the bunker market is gradually adjusting to the prevailing geopolitical environment. With scrubber spreads falling below the psychologically significant USD 100.00 threshold in key bunkering hubs, conventional VLSFO is becoming an increasingly competitive alternative to the 380 HSFO plus scrubber combination, potentially reducing the economic advantage of scrubber-equipped vessels. Ivanov expects the SS Spread to maintain a moderately downward trend in November, although geopolitical developments and bunker fuel price volatility may continue to influence market dynamics. Ivanov commented that in October, the ECA Spread (ES) – the price differential between ULSFO and MGO LS – in Istanbul maintained its moderately downward trend, declining by USD 5.00, from USD 75.00 at the end of September to USD 70.00. However, the index experienced significant fluctuations during the month, ranging between USD 50.00 and USD 100.00. Meanwhile, the monthly average ES value increased by USD 6.25. Overall, the ECA Spread’s sustained position below the USD 100.00 threshold suggests that the market has reached a certain degree of stabilization, despite occasional short-term volatility. According to Ivanov, no significant changes are expected in the ECA Spread dynamics in November, with the index likely to remain relatively stable around its current levels. According to Ivanov, European natural gas prices have surged amid prolonged LNG supply disruptions caused by the Iran conflict and restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. With most Qatari LNG supplies still offline, intensified competition for alternative cargoes pushed European and Asian gas prices in September to their highest levels since the 2022–2023 energy crisis. Although Europe faces no immediate gas shortages, continued supply uncertainty is expected to keep prices elevated, increasing energy costs for households and industry throughout the winter. Ivanov noted that as of October 29, European underground natural gas storage levels continued to increase moderately, reaching 74.89% of total capacity, up 3.63 percentage points from 71.26% at the end of September. Current storage levels were 13.43 percentage points above the beginning-of-year level of 61.46%, but remained below those recorded during the same period last year. Meanwhile, the European natural gas benchmark TTF recorded a sharp increase in October, surging by EUR 24.650/MWh, from EUR 73.938/MWh in September to EUR 98.588/MWh. On October 28, the TTF benchmark briefly exceeded the psychologically significant EUR 100.000/MWh threshold, reflecting heightened volatility and persistent upward pressure on European natural gas prices. According to Ivanov, the price of LNG as a bunker fuel at the port of Sines (Portugal) continued its upward trend in October, rising by USD 401 (USD 2,009/MT compared to USD 1,608/MT at the end of September). Meanwhile, the price differential between LNG and conventional fuel remained in favour of conventional fuel, widening sharply to USD 425 (compared to USD 69 in favour of conventional fuel in September). At the end of October, MGO LS was quoted at USD 1,594/MT in the port of Sines. According to Ivanov, in October, the MABUX Market Differential Index (MDI) – which reflects the correlation between Market Bunker Prices (MBP) and the MABUX Digital Bunker Price Benchmark (DBP) – showed the following trends across the world’s four major bunkering hubs: Rotterdam, Singapore, Fujairah and Houston. In the 380 HSFO segment, Fujairah returned to the undervalued zone, joining Rotterdam and Houston. Average weekly undervaluation levels narrowed by 10 points in Rotterdam and 40 points in Houston, while widening by 11 points in Fujairah. Meanwhile, Singapore shifted into the overvalued zone, becoming the only overvalued port in this fuel segment, with its average premium increasing by 86 points. Houston’s MDI remained above the USD 100.00 mark, while Fujairah’s MDI approached the MBP/DBP price parity level. In the VLSFO segment, Fujairah remained the only overvalued port, although its average premium declined by 19 points. The other three ports stayed in the undervalued zone. Average undervaluation levels widened by 39 points in Rotterdam, remained unchanged in Singapore, and narrowed by 15 points in Houston. Rotterdam’s MDI exceeded the USD 100.00 threshold. In the MGO LS segment, Fujairah shifted into the overvalued zone, becoming the only overvalued port in this fuel category, with its average premium surging by 112 points. The remaining three ports continued to be undervalued. Average undervaluation levels widened by 90 points in Rotterdam and 7 points in Singapore, while narrowing by 11 points in Houston. MDI values in Rotterdam, Singapore and Houston remained above the USD 100.00 mark. Overall, Ivanov commented that the balance between bunker fuel overvaluation and undervaluation across the world’s key bunkering hubs remained mixed in October, with undervaluation continuing to dominate all three fuel segments. The most notable changes were Singapore’s shift into the overvalued zone in the 380 HSFO segment and Fujairah’s transition to overvaluation in the MGO LS segment. Meanwhile, undervaluation intensified primarily in Rotterdam across the VLSFO and MGO LS segments, whereas Houston recorded narrowing discounts across all three fuel grades. Significant discrepancies between MBP and DBP, exceeding USD 100.00 in several ports, indicate persistent imbalances between market bunker prices and the MABUX digital benchmark. Looking ahead to November, Ivanov expects MDI dynamics to remain mixed, with an overall predominance of undervaluation, amid ongoing geopolitical uncertainty and volatility in global energy markets. According to Ivanov, MABUX expects the global bunker market to maintain a firm but highly volatile trend in November, with geopolitical risks and supply constraints continuing to outweigh weakening demand fundamentals. MGO LS and LNG are likely to face the strongest upward price pressure, while HSFO and VLSFO may show mixed regional movements.
takeaways: According to Sergey Ivanov, Director, MABUX, October’s global bunker market remained under strong geopolitical and supply-side pressure.
Middle East tensions, disruptions to oil product flows, tight regional fuel availability and rising LNG prices continued to support bunker quotations.
The key market drivers included: Middle East Conflict: Continued instability around the Strait of Hormuz sustained elevated geopolitical risk premiums, freight costs and bunker price volatility.

articles.title: Ardmore Shipping: Decarbonization through the details
articles.summary: The regulatory requirements governing environmental performance continue to ratchet up, with the EU Emissions Trading System in place for large ships entering EU ports since January 2024, FuelEU Maritime in effect since January 2025 and the IMO’s Carbon Intensity Indicator tightening. At the same time, negotiations...
articles.body: Ardmore Shipping: Decarbonization through the details in International Shipping News 03/11/2026 The regulatory requirements governing environmental performance continue to ratchet up, with the EU Emissions Trading System in place for large ships entering EU ports since January 2024, FuelEU Maritime in effect since January 2025 and the IMO’s Carbon Intensity Indicator tightening. At the same time, negotiations continue over the IMO’s Net Zero Framework. For us, however, efficiency is a long-term operating discipline, not a reaction to each new rule. At year-end 2025, we had 26 product and chemical tankers in operation and our latest Sustainability Report identifies 13 diverse energy efficiency technologies in use on our vessels, from Mewis Ducts and propeller boss cap fins to variable speed drives and low-load boiler optimization, as well as DeepSea’s AI-enabled voyage optimization, and weather-routing services from WetterWelt, all of which combine to support more fuel-efficient operations across the fleet. Garry Noonan, Director, Innovation, Ardmore Shipping In 2025, we also purchased and used biofuel blends of up to B30 to achieve full FuelEU Maritime compliance. Our technical teams and onboard crews made that possible, managing fuel handling, storage and combustion while safeguarding vessel performance throughout the voyages. Their work showed that biofuels can be operationally viable at scale. This progress is borne out in the data. Fleet emissions decreased from 422,083 metric tons of CO2 in 2024 to 361,656 in 2025, a 14% reduction. Trade patterns, waiting time in port, drydocking days and fleet utilization also influence year-on-year emissions, so the decrease cannot be attributed to any single measure. Our focus instead is on sustained improvements in vessel efficiency and fuel consumption. In 2025, our fleet recorded zero Port State Control detentions, and 81% of Port State Control inspections recorded zero deficiencies. This, in turn, is only made possible by our people. Seafarers can access on-demand training through the AFLIX app, use virtual reality to familiarize themselves with vessels before joining, and provide anonymous peer feedback on safety competencies through our Safety Rating app. Every member of our shore-based team also visited a vessel during the year, strengthening the connection between ship and shore. What’s more, our WAVES initiative, which supports women at sea, helped grow our community of women officers from 16 to 25 in 2025. As regulatory requirements evolve, we will keep improving vessel efficiency through practical investment, informed decision-making and the expertise of our people. Technology has an important role to play, but its value depends on how effectively it is integrated into day-to-day vessel operations. That commitment to continuous improvement is central to how we deliver performance and progress. Ardmore Shipping owns and operates a fleet of modern, fuel-efficient product and chemical tankers, delivering energy, mobility and essential commodities in support of global trade. Source: By Garry Noonan, Director, Innovation, Ardmore Shipping 2026-11-03 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Subsea Incidents: Why Preparedness, Technology and Coordination Are Critical to Effective Crisis Response
articles.summary: Subsea incidents may be infrequent, but their consequences can extend far beyond well-control challenges, threatening crew safety, the environment and the continuity of offshore operations. In an exclusive interview with Mr. Mario Fazio, Global Integration Manager and Technical Lead with OSRL, highlights the role of...
articles.body: Subsea Incidents: Why Preparedness, Technology and Coordination Are Critical to Effective Crisis Response in Hellenic Shipping News , Interviews 03/11/2026 S ubsea incidents may be infrequent, but their consequences can extend far beyond well-control challenges, threatening crew safety, the environment and the continuity of offshore operations. In an exclusive interview with Mr. Mario Fazio, Global Integration Manager and Technical Lead with OSRL, highlights the role of specialised technology, rapid equipment mobilisation and coordination among key stakeholders in strengthening emergency response capabilities. Mr. Fazio also explains why thorough advance planning, digital tools and artificial intelligence must work alongside human expertise and sound judgement to ensure an effective response when every hour matters. 1. OSRL describes these incidents as low-frequency but high-consequence. From the perspective of the maritime and offshore industries, what risk is most often underestimated when a subsea incident cannot be brought under control quickly? One of the most underestimated risks is the way a subsea incident can rapidly escalate beyond a well-control challenge into a much broader operational, environmental and stakeholder management event. The longer an incident remains uncontrolled, the greater the potential for impacts on people, the environment, offshore operations, supply chains and public confidence. Another important consideration is the complexity involved in coordinating specialist equipment, vessels, personnel and decision-making under significant time pressure. That is why preparedness is so important. Having response plans, logistics arrangements and specialist capabilities in place before an incident occurs can make a significant difference to how effectively the industry responds when every hour matters. 2. In practical terms, how could this new capability affect response times, the safety of the vessels and crews involved, and the ability to limit environmental and operational impacts? The capability has been designed to provide operators with additional flexibility in shallow-water scenarios where conventional vertical deployment methods may not be possible or may introduce additional risks. By enabling deployment and lowering of a capping stack from an offset location outside the hazardous surface plume, it helps support safer operations for vessels and personnel involved in the response. From a preparedness perspective, having a response-ready capability that can be mobilised rapidly and integrated into established response arrangements can help reduce uncertainty and improve confidence in deployment planning. Ultimately, any capability that supports safe and controlled source-control operations contributes to industry’s ability to minimise potential environmental and operational consequences during an incident. Fazio, Mario Global Response Integration Manager, OSRL Australia 3. Equipment alone is not enough during a real emergency. What level of preparedness and coordination is required in advance between OSRL, offshore operators, specialist vessel providers, ports and the relevant authorities? Effective response starts long before an incident occurs. Equipment is only one part of the equation. Organisations also need engineering studies, source-control planning, logistics execution planning, exercises and clear governance arrangements to ensure everyone understands their role during an emergency. A successful response depends on close coordination between operators, response organisations, specialist vessel providers, ports, regulatory authorities and technical experts. The objective is to establish practical mobilisation pathways, understand regional logistics constraints, and validate response strategies before they are needed. When those relationships and plans are developed in advance, organisations are far better positioned to respond effectively under pressure. 4. The new system can be mobilised from OSRL’s base in Norway by sea or air. How achievable is rapid deployment across different regions, and what are the main logistical challenges involved? Rapid deployment is achievable, but it depends on extensive planning and preparation. The equipment has been designed for mobilisation by sea and air, and its location in Norway provides access to established transport infrastructure and specialist logistics networks. The challenge is not simply moving equipment from one place to another. A response may involve vessel availability, aircraft capacity, customs requirements, port and airport infrastructure, regulatory approvals, specialist personnel and local operating conditions. This is why logistics execution planning forms such an important part of source-control preparedness. Understanding these factors in advance helps reduce uncertainty and supports faster, more coordinated mobilisation when an incident occurs. 5. How are simulations, digital technologies and artificial intelligence already changing preparedness and decision-making during such incidents, and where does human judgement remain indispensable? Digital technologies are helping organisations strengthen preparedness by improving modelling, planning, logistics analysis and training. Simulation tools can help operators better understand potential incident scenarios, assess response options and validate response plans before an event occurs. Increasingly, data-driven technologies are providing faster access to information that can support operational decision-making. However, human judgement remains essential. Every incident is unique and decision-makers must balance technical, operational, environmental and regulatory considerations, often with incomplete information and changing conditions. Technology can inform decisions, but experienced responders, engineers and incident management teams remain critical to interpreting information, assessing risk and determining the most appropriate course of action. The most effective approach is one that combines advanced technology with experienced people and well-rehearsed response arrangements. articles.title: Alternative-fuel ships outpace port readiness, new LR report finds
articles.summary: Alternative-fuel vessel orders are outpacing the development of the port infrastructure needed to support them, according to a new global study by Lloyd’s Register (LR), highlighting a growing gap between ship capability and fuel availability. LR’s new Fuel for Thought: Ports report finds that 1,942...
articles.body: Alternative-fuel ships outpace port readiness, new LR report finds in International Shipping News 03/11/2026 A lternative-fuel vessel orders are outpacing the development of the port infrastructure needed to support them, according to a new global study by Lloyd’s Register (LR), highlighting a growing gap between ship capability and fuel availability. LR’s new Fuel for Thought: Ports report finds that 1,942 alternative-fuel-capable vessels were on order in January 2026, with alternative-fuel ships representing 47% of global orderbook tonnage, according to Clarksons Research. Yet readiness differs sharply by fuel: LNG bunkering was available at 222 ports, compared with just 25 actively offering methanol, while the first commercial ammonia bunkering operation, at Ulsan in South Korea, was completed only in April 2026. The gap is particularly stark for emerging fuels. LR identified 385 methanol-capable and 45 ammonia-capable vessels on order, while the infrastructure and low-carbon fuel supply needed to serve them remains concentrated among a relatively small number of ports. Most ports pursuing ammonia remain at pilot, trial or safety-framework stage. The report concludes that fuel choice and trade route are now inseparable, with newbuild and conversion decisions needing to reflect the availability of fuel at the ports vessels will actually use. Kamran Ul Haq, Senior Vice President, LR Ports Advisory, said: “The fleet is moving faster than the infrastructure needed to support it. An owner can order an alternative-fuel vessel today, but that does not mean the fuel will be available where that ship needs it. Fuel strategy and trading strategy can no longer be considered separately. “Ports do not need to back every fuel. They need to understand where credible demand will emerge and put the safety, regulation, skills and partnerships in place to respond. Ports that make those decisions early will be better positioned as alternative-fuel volumes grow.” The report shows that the transition is developing at markedly different speeds by fuel. LNG already has a mature, near-global bunkering network, while biofuel blends are the most immediately deployable option because they can largely move through existing bunker infrastructure. Methanol is becoming commercially established at a small number of major ports, while ammonia has moved from demonstrations into commercial bunkering at Ulsan but remains at an earlier stage elsewhere. Hydrogen remains largely a short-sea and demonstration fuel. The research also points to a geographically concentrated transition, with many of the commercial and near-commercial milestones identified clustered around Northern Europe, North Asia and Singapore. This reinforces the need for owners to assess fuel availability along individual trade routes rather than rely on global measures of alternative-fuel readiness. For fuels that can use established infrastructure, the picture is more mature. LR’s Fuel Oil Bunker Analysis and Advisory Service (FOBAS) data recorded drop-in biofuel deliveries at 90 ports worldwide over the previous 12 months. The 13 leading ports accounted for 77.5% of bunker quantities recorded, with Singapore alone representing more than a quarter. Safety, regulation and workforce capability will also determine how quickly ports can move from trials to routine supply. The report identifies berth-specific risk assessment, appropriate licensing, emergency preparedness and trained personnel as recurring foundations behind successful alternative-fuel operations Kamran Ul Haq adds: “For ports, investment should follow credible demand rather than trying to prepare for every fuel at once. Named vessel programmes and green shipping corridors are also ways to reduce infrastructure risk, alongside early investment in safety frameworks, licensing, emergency preparedness and workforce skills.” LR Fuel for Thought: Ports forms part of LR’s wider award-winning Fuel for Thought series, which provides independent, technical insight into the alternative fuels shaping shipping’s transition to lower carbon operations. The report is intended to support informed decision-making across the ports sector as it navigates the complexities of maritime energy transition. Source: Lloyd’s Register Tops 2026-11-03 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

Most ports pursuing ammonia remain at pilot, trial or safety-framework stage.

articles.body: Baltic Dry Index Slips to Near 1-Week Low in Dry Bulk Market , International Shipping News 03/11/2026 The Baltic Exchange’s dry bulk freight index, which tracks rates for ships carrying dry bulk commodities, snapped its three-day winning streak on Monday, dropping by 2.4% to its lowest since October 27 at 2,648 points. Declines were seen across all vessel segments. The capesize index, which typically transports 150,000-ton cargoes, including iron ore and coal, slipped nearly 4% to 3,963 points, after three consecutive sessions of advances. At the same time, the panamax index, which usually carries 60,000 to 70,000 tons of coal or grain, decreased by 0.8% to its lowest since April 13 at 1,874 points, extending its losing streak to 14 consecutive sessions. Among smaller vessels, the supramax index fell by 0.5% to a fresh low since October 15 at 1,856 points. Source: Trading Economics 2026-11-03 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Could India’s steel ‘Vision 2047’ create the next breakthrough for dry bulk demand?
articles.summary: The government of India’s newly released draft National Steel Policy ‘Vision 2047’ targets 531 million tonnes of crude steel production, 772 million tonnes of iron ore demand and 236 million tonnes of coking coal demand by 2047. If these numbers are achieved, India could emerge as the largest source of incremental...
articles.body: Could India’s steel ‘Vision 2047’ create the next breakthrough for dry bulk demand? in Dry Bulk Market , International Shipping News 03/11/2026 T he government of India’s newly released draft National Steel Policy ‘Vision 2047’ targets 531 million tonnes of crude steel production, 772 million tonnes of iron ore demand and 236 million tonnes of coking coal demand by 2047. If these numbers are achieved, India could emerge as the largest source of incremental seaborne demand for steelmaking raw materials, reshaping iron ore, coking coal and dry bulk shipping markets over the next two decades. On 10 October 2026, the government released the draft National Steel Policy: Vision 2047 for public consultation, with ambitious targets. The vision projects steelmaking capacity to surge from the current 220 million tonnes to 604 million tonnes by 2047, while crude steel production is expected to reach 531 million tonnes (up from 164 million tonnes in 2025). The policy also projects annual iron ore demand of 772 million tonnes, coking coal demand of 236 million tonnes and scrap consumption of 123 million tonnes. India’s crude steel production For dry bulk shipping, the key question is not whether India can produce more steel. The country has established itself as the world’s second-largest steel producer. The more important question is whether India can secure the enormous quantities of raw materials required to support this expansion, and where those raw materials will come from. In our previous analysis, we had highlighted that India’s iron ore market was undergoing a structural transition. As domestic steelmakers are absorbing a larger share of locally produced ore, exports are declining and imports are rising. Iron ore exports fell from 52 million tonnes in 2020 to 27 million tonnes in 2025, while imports increased to more than 12 million tonnes. The shift was beginning to support longer-haul imports from Brazil and increasing the role of Capesize vessels in India’s import trade. The new policy suggests this trend could accelerate considerably. India produced a record 289 million tonnes of iron ore in FY2024-25 compared to 204 million tonnes in FY2020-21. While the country has one of the largest iron ore reserves in the world, increasing annual production to a level capable of supporting 772 million tonnes of demand would require unprecedented expansion in mining, beneficiation, rail infrastructure and slurry pipelines. Even under an optimistic scenario, domestic production may struggle to keep pace with the steel sector’s expansion. If India manages to increase iron ore production to around 550-600 million tonnes by 2047, the country could still face a supply gap of 170-220 million tonnes annually. Under such a scenario, iron ore imports are likely to approach 200 million tonnes per year, transforming India from a marginal importer into one of the world’s largest iron ore destination markets. At the same time, exports could become negligible as domestic steelmakers consume increasing quantities of fines and lower-grade ores that were previously exported. However, the relationship is becoming increasingly complicated between steel production and demand for raw materials because of changes in steelmaking technology. A transition towards electric arc furnaces (EAFs) appears bearish for iron ore and coking coal demand because traditional EAF steelmaking is primarily based on scrap. This is largely true in Europe and North America, where electric furnaces are fed predominantly by recycled steel. India is different Many Indian EAF and induction furnace operators rely heavily on direct reduced iron (DRI), commonly known as sponge iron, alongside scrap. Unlike scrap-based steelmaking, DRI production still requires substantial quantities of iron ore. In India, much of this DRI is produced through coal-based processes, meaning that a shift towards electric furnaces does not eliminate raw-material demand in the same way it does in mature scrap-rich economies. This distinction is important because it explains why the government’s projections still show strong growth in iron ore and coking coal requirements despite a possible shift towards EAF. The draft policy expects scrap consumption to expand from 36 million tonnes in FY2025-26 to 123 million tonnes by 2047, equivalent to around 21% of projected crude steel production. The government also expects domestic scrap collection to rise substantially through vehicle recycling, ship recycling and a more formalised scrap collection industry. Nevertheless, scrap availability is unlikely to remove the need for large-scale imports of steelmaking raw materials. India currently consumes more scrap than it generates domestically and already relies on imports. Several industry studies suggest that global scrap availability may tighten over time as major exporting countries retain more material to support their own decarbonisation efforts. The government’s own projections acknowledge this limitation. Despite the increase in scrap consumption to 123 million tonnes, the policy still expects iron ore demand to reach substantial amounts by 2047. Coking coal may ultimately become as important a shipping story as iron ore. Drewry forecasts India’s coking coal imports to rise from 68.6 million tonnes in 2025 to 80.3 million tonnes by 2031. However, the draft steel policy projects total coking coal demand of 236 million tonnes by 2047. Currently, India imports around 92% of its coking coal requirement, and its import needs could increase dramatically even if domestic production and coal washing capacity improve. Assuming import dependence declines moderately to 80-90%, India’s annual coking coal imports could reach 190-210 million tonnes by 2047. That would be more than triple current import levels and establish India as the dominant source of incremental seaborne coking coal demand globally. The source of these imports will determine the full shipping impact. Brazil appears well-positioned to increase its share of India’s iron ore imports as demand for higher-grade ore rises. Guinea’s Simandou project could become another important supplier as its 120 million tonnes of planned exports gradually enter the market. The proposed Central African Republic-Kribi corridor could create an additional source of Atlantic Basin iron ore supply if the project progresses as planned. We previously estimated that the corridor could support more than 90 million tonnes of annual exports and generate demand for 70-80 Capesize vessels. Long-haul imports from Brazil, Guinea, and potentially Central Africa are likely to boost tonne-mile demand more than Australian cargoes. This would strengthen Capesize utilisation and increase demand for vessels across the market. The coking coal trade could have an even broader impact on the fleet. Australia is likely to remain India’s largest supplier, but rising imports from Canada, the US and Mozambique could create additional opportunities for both Capesize and Panamax vessels. Meanwhile, any increase in scrap imports would generate employment for Handysize and Supramax ships. Conclusion India’s Steel Vision 2047 is ultimately a shipping story. The policy projects greater use of scrap, increased electrification and lower-emission steelmaking technologies. However, unlike Europe and North America, India’s electric steel sector remains closely linked to direct reduced iron production, meaning that demand for iron ore and coal is likely to remain substantial even as EAF capacity expands. If India achieves the ambitions outlined in the draft policy, iron ore exports could largely disappear. At the same time, growing scrap requirements could create an additional import market. Even though China will remain the world’s largest iron ore importer for the foreseeable future, its steel market is increasingly mature. Meanwhile, India is still in the early stages of a multi-decade industrial expansion. If India achieves its 2047 targets, it could become the largest source of incremental seaborne demand for steelmaking raw materials and one of the most important long-term growth drivers for the global dry bulk shipping market. Source: Drewry Tops 2026-11-03 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

The policy also projects annual iron ore demand of 772 million tonnes, coking coal demand of 236 million tonnes and scrap consumption of 123 million tonnes.
India’s crude steel production For dry bulk shipping, the key question is not whether India can produce more steel.

articles.body: MABUX: Global Bunker Market To Maintain A Firm But Highly Volatile Trend In November in International Shipping News 03/11/2026 October’s global bunker market remained under strong geopolitical and supply-side pressure. Middle East tensions, disruptions to oil product flows, tight regional fuel availability and rising LNG prices continued to support bunker quotations. The key market drivers included: • Middle East Conflict: Continued instability around the Strait of Hormuz sustained elevated geopolitical risk premiums, freight costs and bunker price volatility. • Crude Oil Supply Constraints: Disrupted Gulf oil exports, limited supply flexibility and higher transportation costs maintained upward pressure on crude and marine fuel prices. • Tight Distillate Supply: Restricted gasoil availability and strong refinery margins continued to support MGO LS prices, widening premiums over residual bunker fuels. • Regional Fuel Imbalances: Limited HSFO and VLSFO availability, particularly in Asian bunkering hubs, contributed to significant regional price differentials and changes in scrubber spreads. • Higher Bunker Transportation Costs: Elevated tanker freight rates constrained fuel arbitrage flows between Europe and Asia, increasing supply pressure in major bunkering hubs. • Rising LNG Prices: Tight global LNG supply, stronger European gas prices and seasonal demand expectations reduced LNG’s competitiveness against conventional marine fuels. • Alternative Fuel Transition: Continued expansion of dual-fuel and battery-powered fleets supported the longer-term diversification of marine fuel demand, although high alternative fuel costs remained a constraint. In October, the MABUX 380 HSFO Index extended its upward trend, gaining USD 76.75, from USD 701.67/MT at the end of September to USD 778.42/MT. The VLSFO Index rose by USD 70.81, reaching USD 913.07/MT compared to USD 842.26/MT a month earlier, breaking above the USD 900/MT threshold. Meanwhile, the MGO LS Index recorded only a marginal increase of USD 2.62, edging up from USD 1,521.88/MT at the end of September to USD 1,524.50/MT. The upward trend in bunker prices during October was primarily driven by the continued escalation of the military conflict between the United States and Iran, which sustained a substantial geopolitical risk premium in global crude oil and refined petroleum product prices. At the time of reporting, MABUX bunker indices remained close to their peak levels, reflecting persistent geopolitical tensions and elevated uncertainty across global energy markets. The MABUX Global Scrubber Spread (SS) – the price differential between 380 HSFO and VLSFO – continued its moderate downward trend in October, declining by USD 5.94, from USD 140.59 at the end of September to USD 134.65, while remaining above the USD 100.00 SS Benchmark. The monthly average SS value also decreased by USD 23.78. In Rotterdam, the SS Spread increased by USD 11.00, from USD 57.00 at the end of September to USD 68.00, remaining below the USD 100.00 threshold. However, the monthly average SS value declined by USD 25.63. In Singapore, the 380 HSFO/VLSFO price differential narrowed by USD 35.00, from USD 125.00 in September to USD 90.00, falling below the USD 100.00 benchmark and briefly dropping to as low as USD 20.00 during the month. The port’s monthly average SS value also recorded a substantial decline of USD 80.33. The continued narrowing of the SS Spread suggests that the bunker market is gradually adjusting to the prevailing geopolitical environment. With scrubber spreads falling below the psychologically significant USD 100.00 threshold in key bunkering hubs, conventional VLSFO is becoming an increasingly competitive alternative to the 380 HSFO plus scrubber combination, potentially reducing the economic advantage of scrubber-equipped vessels. We expect the SS Spread to maintain a moderately downward trend in November, although geopolitical developments and bunker fuel price volatility may continue to influence market dynamics. More detailed information is available in the Differentials section at mabux.com. In October, the ECA Spread (ES) – the price differential between ULSFO and MGO LS – in Istanbul maintained its moderately downward trend, declining by USD 5.00, from USD 75.00 at the end of September to USD 70.00. However, the index experienced significant fluctuations during the month, ranging between USD 50.00 and USD 100.00. Meanwhile, the monthly average ES value increased by USD 6.25. Overall, the ECA Spread’s sustained position below the USD 100.00 threshold suggests that the market has reached a certain degree of stabilization, despite occasional short-term volatility. We expect no significant changes in the ECA Spread dynamics in November, with the index likely to remain relatively stable around its current levels. More detailed information is available in the Differentials section at mabux.com. European natural gas prices have surged amid prolonged LNG supply disruptions caused by the Iran conflict and restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. With most Qatari LNG supplies still offline, intensified competition for alternative cargoes pushed European and Asian gas prices in September to their highest levels since the 2022–2023 energy crisis. Although Europe faces no immediate gas shortages, continued supply uncertainty is expected to keep prices elevated, increasing energy costs for households and industry throughout the winter. As of October 29, European underground natural gas storage levels continued to increase moderately, reaching 74.89% of total capacity, up 3.63 percentage points from 71.26% at the end of September. Current storage levels were 13.43 percentage points above the beginning-of-year level of 61.46%, but remained below those recorded during the same period last year. Meanwhile, the European natural gas benchmark TTF recorded a sharp increase in October, surging by EUR 24.650/MWh, from EUR 73.938/MWh in September to EUR 98.588/MWh. On October 28, the TTF benchmark briefly exceeded the psychologically significant EUR 100.000/MWh threshold, reflecting heightened volatility and persistent upward pressure on European natural gas prices. The price of LNG as a bunker fuel at the port of Sines (Portugal) continued its upward trend in October, rising by USD 401 (USD 2,009/MT compared to USD 1,608/MT at the end of September). Meanwhile, the price differential between LNG and conventional fuel remained in favour of conventional fuel, widening sharply to USD 425 (compared to USD 69 in favour of conventional fuel in September). At the end of October, MGO LS was quoted at USD 1,594/MT in the port of Sines. More detailed information is available in the “LNG Bunkering” section at mabux.com. In October, the MABUX Market Differential Index (MDI) – which reflects the correlation between Market Bunker Prices (MBP) and the MABUX Digital Bunker Price Benchmark (DBP) – showed the following trends across the world’s four major bunkering hubs: Rotterdam, Singapore, Fujairah and Houston. In the 380 HSFO segment, Fujairah returned to the undervalued zone, joining Rotterdam and Houston. Average weekly undervaluation levels narrowed by 10 points in Rotterdam and 40 points in Houston, while widening by 11 points in Fujairah. Meanwhile, Singapore shifted into the overvalued zone, becoming the only overvalued port in this fuel segment, with its average premium increasing by 86 points. Houston’s MDI remained above the USD 100.00 mark, while Fujairah’s MDI approached the MBP/DBP price parity level. In the VLSFO segment, Fujairah remained the only overvalued port, although its average premium declined by 19 points. The other three ports stayed in the undervalued zone. Average undervaluation levels widened by 39 points in Rotterdam, remained unchanged in Singapore, and narrowed by 15 points in Houston. Rotterdam’s MDI exceeded the USD 100.00 threshold. In the MGO LS segment, Fujairah shifted into the overvalued zone, becoming the only overvalued port in this fuel category, with its average premium surging by 112 points. The remaining three ports continued to be undervalued. Average undervaluation levels widened by 90 points in Rotterdam and 7 points in Singapore, while narrowing by 11 points in Houston. MDI values in Rotterdam, Singapore and Houston remained above the USD 100.00 mark. Overall, the balance between bunker fuel overvaluation and undervaluation across the world’s key bunkering hubs remained mixed in October, with undervaluation continuing to dominate all three fuel segments. The most notable changes were Singapore’s shift into the overvalued zone in the 380 HSFO segment and Fujairah’s transition to overvaluation in the MGO LS segment. Meanwhile, undervaluation intensified primarily in Rotterdam across the VLSFO and MGO LS segments, whereas Houston recorded narrowing discounts across all three fuel grades. Significant discrepancies between MBP and DBP, exceeding USD 100.00 in several ports, indicate persistent imbalances between market bunker prices and the MABUX digital benchmark. Looking ahead to November, we expect MDI dynamics to remain mixed, with an overall predominance of undervaluation, amid ongoing geopolitical uncertainty and volatility in global energy markets. More detailed information on the correlation between market bunker prices and the MABUX digital benchmark is available in the Digital Bunker Prices section at mabux.com. Other Global Bunkering Trends: • EU Methane Regulation: The European Parliament backed a three-year delay to key requirements for oil, gas and coal importers, extending the European Commission’s proposed one-year postponement. The extension would not apply to imports restricted by EU sanctions. • Dual-Fuel Fleet: According to the World Shipping Council (WSC), the global dual-fuel fleet expanded by 41% year-on-year to 503 vessels, with another 849 on order, bringing the combined total to 1,352 ships. • LNG Bunkering: Wood Mackenzie forecasts that LNG will displace over 400,000 barrels per day of conventional oil-based bunker demand by 2030, becoming the main driver of marine fuel demand growth during the near-term energy transition. • Nuclear-Powered Shipping: Lloyd’s Register and the British Ports Association urged ports to prepare for advanced nuclear technologies, including nuclear-powered vessels and small modular reactors (SMRs). Regulatory, insurance and safety challenges remain major obstacles. • Battery-Powered Fleet: According to ZESTAs, the number of battery-powered ships in operation or under construction has surged by 258% since 2023. As of October 2026, 2,124 vessels were operational, with another 925 under construction. • Global shipbuilding order book: According to BIMCO, the global shipbuilding order book rose by 13% year-on-year to 203.2 million CGT, remaining close to May’s record high of 210.4 million CGT. China continues to dominate the sector, securing 74% of new orders over the past year and accounting for 64% of the global order book, followed by South Korea (19%) and Japan (6%). MABUX expects the global bunker market to maintain a firm but highly volatile trend in November, with geopolitical risks and supply constraints continuing to outweigh weakening demand fundamentals. MGO LS and LNG are likely to face the strongest upward price pressure, while HSFO and VLSFO may show mixed regional movements. articles.body: Fuel Switch Snapshot: Pooling slump erases LBM’s edge over LNG in International Shipping News 03/11/2026 Liquefied biomethane (LBM) has flipped from a $2/mt discount to LNG to a $48/mt premium over it in Rotterdam for vessels with Otto medium speed (Otto MS) engines. For vessels with diesel slow speed (diesel SS) engines, it has flipped from a $6/mt discount to a $43/mt premium. OceanScore’s FuelEU pooling index has fallen by €15.35/mtCO2e ($17/mtCO2e) to €80.45/mtCO2e ($90/mtCO2e) over the past week. This has cut the potential pooling value of LBM’s compliance surplus by $53-62/mt on intra-EU voyages, against $0-9/mt for LNG. LBM prices have gained $133-141/mt depending on engine type, and LNG prices $84-92/mt over the past week. The lower potential pooling value of LBM’s compliance surplus has added to the rise in LBM prices and undercut their edge over LNG. LSMGO has slid in Rotterdam while both gaseous fuels have climbed, flipping its premiums of $73/mt over LNG (diesel SS) and $79/mt over LBM (diesel SS) to discounts of $94/mt and $137/mt. LSMGO’s discounts to LNG (Otto MS) and LBM (Otto MS) have widened by $158/mt and $208/mt to $202/mt and $249/mt. Liquid fuels Rotterdam’s LSMGO has fallen by $74/mt over the past week, while HSFO has gained $21/mt and VLSFO has dipped by $1/mt. B100 has edged up by $5/mt in Rotterdam, as the potential pooling value of its compliance surplus has dropped by $51/mt. Its discount to VLSFO has narrowed by $5/mt to $133/mt. B30-VLSFO is at a $66/mt discount to VLSFO in Rotterdam and B30-LSMGO is at a $134/mt discount to LSMGO. Dutch ZRE A tickets have fallen by €5/mtCO2e ($6/mtCO2e) to €235/mtCO2e ($263/mtCO2e) over the past week. In Singapore, LSMGO has slumped by $120/mt, HSFO has lost $37/mt and VLSFO has gained $22/mt. The port’s B100 has gained $71/mt, and its premium over VLSFO has widened by $49/mt to $396/mt. B30-VLSFO is at a $92/mt premium over VLSFO. Liquid gases Rotterdam’s LNG prices have risen by $84-92/mt depending on engine type, even though the TTF contract they are priced on has moved from November to December delivery. That move has taken $39/mt off the price. Excluding it, LNG (Otto MS) has risen by $123/mt and LNG (diesel SS) by $132/mt. Rotterdam’s LBM prices have climbed by $133-141/mt depending on engine type over the same period. Singapore’s LNG prices have risen by $63-67/mt depending on engine type. articles.title: Slowing Intra-Asia Chemical, Palms Spot Freight Fixtures Deter Trades
articles.summary: Tanker freight in Asia beating popular expectations by staying buoyant into November could hinder chemical and palms cargo flows throughout the rest of the fourth quarter. • Liquid bulk shipping costs climb despite fleet growth • El Nino supply jitters prolong palms freight uptick • Tanker pile-up at ports curtails...
articles.body: Slowing Intra-Asia Chemical, Palms Spot Freight Fixtures Deter Trades in International Shipping News 03/11/2026 Tanker freight in Asia beating popular expectations by staying buoyant into November could hinder chemical and palms cargo flows throughout the rest of the fourth quarter. • Liquid bulk shipping costs climb despite fleet growth • El Nino supply jitters prolong palms freight uptick • Tanker pile-up at ports curtails SE Asia, India tonnage supply Freight indications having already advanced since September have further increased into November despite new vessel additions and pre-Diwali holiday restocking in India tapering off. Diwali or Festival of Light is a major Hindu holiday in India. During the two-week period to 28 October, ICIS-assessed chemical and palms freight indications have risen on most intra-Asia trade lanes. Palms freight for shipments from southeast Asia to India, as well as China soared to the highest levels in more than three years. Palms exports from Malaysia for H1 October expanded by 43.2% to 58.3% month on month as a traditional uptick in pre-Diwali restocking kicked in. Separately, rising crude oil prices also enhanced palm oil’s competitiveness as a biodiesel feedstock, buoying regional palms trades beyond the seasonal increase in activity. “Palms traders that have been overly conservative during H1 2026 are also ramping up trading activities ahead of year-end financial book closures,” one shipbroker noted. Palms freight is benefiting from knee-jerk inventory building activities both in India and China stoked by supply jitters in the two largest consuming countries that have been linked to the ongoing El Nino phenomenon. The El Nino phenomenon of extreme dry weather and drought in the Asia Pacific is expected to reduce yields from plantations and disrupt palm oil production in Malaysia and Indonesia into 2027. Unlike for palms freight, supply-demand forces tied to regional chemical trades have been mixed, thus far reflected in uneven freight indications across trade lanes. Active gasoline blending trades are still bolstering southbound chemical freight indications, which continue to outperform those for northbound, intra-southeast Asia and intra-northeast Asia trade lanes. Whether it be for palms or chemical shipments, however, tanker spaces have become and could remain challenging to secure into November and even beyond. “Freight [for liquid bulk] is a headache now [especially] for part parcel cargoes,” a trader active in southbound trades separately lamented during the week ended 28 October. Such challenges, which have become prevalent in the wider market, run contrary to one dominant view earlier this year. Back then, shipping veterans had suggested that with newbuild tankers entering service hitting multi-year high, liquid bulk freight, including for chemical and palms shipments, should come under pressure in 2026. Yet, tanker freight indications have not eased even for palms shipments after pre-Diwali restocking lost steam. Sentiment also remained bullish in the chemical freight market. Shipowners have even pulled back from letting out tanker spaces on spot basis, banking on freight indications to further improve into November, a second shipbroker observed. Such bullish expectations build upon two positive indicators. Clean tanker rates have continued to hover around record levels not just because the Middle East war has improved arbitrage for trades within Asia. Tankers previously earmarked for clean petroleum products have also been diverted to ship crude and other dirty products. Tanker freight also drew support from unrelenting cost inflationary pressure. Marine fuel costs in Singapore, the world’s top bunkering hub, generally climbed since mid-September, nearly touching $1,000/tonne on 27 October, based on industry data. In southeast Asia and India, tanker supply is still being compromised by severe disruptions to vessel schedules attributed to still ongoing port congestions. “Tankers holding gasoline blending cargoes were seen waiting for more than 10 days to berth at a petrochemical hub,” a third shipbroker noted. articles.title: FMC to Host Demurrage and Detention Research Symposium
articles.summary: The Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) will host a research symposium on March 31, 2027, at its headquarters in Washington, D.C. This event will bring together scholars conducting research on demurrage and detention (DnD) practices and policies…
articles.body: FMC to Host Demurrage and Detention Research Symposium Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 2, 2026 © Adobe Stock/lunamarina The Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) will host a research symposium on March 31, 2027, at its headquarters in Washington, D.C. This event will bring together scholars conducting research on demurrage and detention (DnD) practices and policies, as well as industry experts who will share insights regarding the use of DnD to incentivize cargo fluidity and velocity. The symposium will foster research and discussion that can advance the understanding of DnD practices and their broader economic and operational implications for freight fluidity. The symposium will focus on the following overarching research question: What economic theories or quantifiable frameworks can be developed and used to evaluate the relationships among compensatory costs, DnD charge levels, and the behavioral responses necessary to effectively incentivize cargo movement and freight fluidity? The FMC is now accepting submission from individuals interested in sharing their papers examining the policies and effects of DnD. The Commission especially encourages the submission of papers that develop and/or evaluate methodologies for setting DnD charges above compensatory costs in order to maintain and demonstrate an effective incentive. Papers may also develop or examine methodologies to assess behavioral responses to DnD charges and how those responses can be deployed to improve cargo velocity and freight fluidity. Key dates Deadline for submissions – February 15, 2027 Notification to author(s) – March 1, 2027 Registration opens and agenda announced – March 1, 2027 Research symposium – March 31, 2027 The research symposium will focus on the following key themes and questions: Overall incentivizing mechanism: Establish a quantifiable economic framework for determining whether, and by how much, DnD charges must differ from actual compensatory costs to effectively incentivize the desired behavioral responses. Identify controllable and uncontrollable factors associated with DnD and evaluate how these factors affect charge levels, compensatory costs, and incentive effectiveness. DnD charges: What factors impact the effectiveness of DnD charges as financial incentives? Examine how DnD terms and rates are negotiated and determine how contractual relationships, the Incoterms, and/or government holds influence the level and structure of DnD charges. Examine decision-making alignment across relevant parties, including whether the party that controls the relevant operational behavior is consistently the party that bears the financial consequences of DnD charges. Compensatory costs: How should compensatory costs associated with DnD be identified, measured, and quantified? How can one deploy a quantifiable framework for compensatory costs, including actual costs and opportunity costs, associated with DnD and identify the factors that influence those costs? Behavioral changes: What is the demonstrated relationship between increases in DnD charges and incremental improvements in the desired behavior, and at what point do diminishing returns occur? Examine how behavioral responses to DnD incentives translate into improvements in cargo velocity and overall freight fluidity. If you are interested in submitting a paper, please send an executive summary, extended abstract, or completed paper by February 15, 2027, to Grace Wang at [email protected] . You will receive an email confirming receipt of your submission. Preference to participate in the symposium will be given to completed papers. Accepted participants should expect to receive notification by March 1, 2027. For those interested in attending the conference as audience members, registration will open March 1, 2027 . This symposium will be held at FMC Headquarters: 800 North Capitol Street, N.W. Washington, D.C., 20573. For more information or questions, please contact Grace Wang at [email protected] and Melina Reilly at [email protected] .

articles.summary: The global shipping industry is ordering alternative-fuel vessels faster than ports can develop the infrastructure needed to fuel them, according to a new report from Lloyd’s Register (LR), highlighting a...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network The world’s first green methanol fueled container ship has bunkered in the Port of Rotterdam, taking on OCI HyFuels green methanol for the final leg of its maiden voyage. Photo credit: Port of Rotterdam The global shipping industry is ordering alternative-fuel vessels faster than ports can develop the infrastructure needed to fuel them, according to a new report from Lloyd’s Register (LR), highlighting a growing challenge for shipowners investing in cleaner propulsion technologies. LR’s new Fuel for Thought: Ports report, released Monday, found that 1,942 alternative-fuel-capable vessels were on order as of January 2026, representing 47% of the global orderbook by tonnage, according to Clarksons Research. But the infrastructure needed to support those ships varies dramatically depending on the fuel. Liquefied natural gas (LNG) bunkering was available at 222 ports worldwide, compared with just 25 ports actively offering methanol. Commercial ammonia bunkering, meanwhile, has been recorded at only one port, following the first operation at Ulsan, South Korea, in April 2026. The disparity is particularly significant given that shipowners have ordered 385 methanol-capable vessels and 45 ammonia-capable ships, according to LR. “The fleet is moving faster than the infrastructure needed to support it,” said Kamran Ul Haq, Senior Vice President of LR Ports Advisory. “An owner can order an alternative-fuel vessel today, but that does not mean the fuel will be available where that ship needs it. Fuel strategy and trading strategy can no longer be considered separately.” The findings come amid a renewed surge in alternative-fuel vessel orders, led overwhelmingly by LNG. As gCaptain reported in October , data from DNV’s Alternative Fuels Insight platform showed that shipowners ordered 69 alternative-fuel vessels in September, the highest monthly total in nearly two years. LNG accounted for 48 of those orders, with new contracts spanning containerships, car carriers, bulk carriers and ro-ro vessels. The surge brought alternative-fuel orders to 311 vessels through the first nine months of 2026, up 53% from the same period a year earlier. LNG’s dominance reflects its relative maturity compared with emerging alternatives. With an established global supply network and commercially proven propulsion technology, LNG offers shipowners greater flexibility when deploying vessels across international trading routes. Methanol, by comparison, is gaining ground at major bunkering hubs but remains limited in geographic reach. Ammonia is still at an earlier stage, with most ports pursuing the fuel focused on pilot projects, safety assessments and regulatory frameworks. The challenge is particularly relevant for ports deciding where to invest. Last week, gCaptain reported that the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach identified LNG and methanol as the most viable alternative marine fuels for the near and medium term. Their joint Clean Marine Fuel Feasibility Assessment recommended a phased approach to infrastructure development, relying on existing ship-to-ship bunkering capabilities for LNG while pursuing methanol pilot projects and improvements to safety and permitting requirements. The Southern California findings closely mirror LR’s conclusion that ports should focus on fuels with credible demand rather than attempt to accommodate every emerging technology. “Ports do not need to back every fuel,” Ul Haq said. “They need to understand where credible demand will emerge and put the safety, regulation, skills and partnerships in place to respond.” LR also found that alternative-fuel infrastructure remains concentrated in a relatively small number of shipping hubs, particularly Northern Europe, North Asia and Singapore. That concentration makes access to fuel along specific trade routes increasingly important when owners evaluate newbuildings and vessel conversions. Biofuels offer a more immediate alternative because compatible blends can generally be supplied through existing bunker infrastructure. LR’s Fuel Oil Bunker Analysis and Advisory Service recorded drop-in biofuel deliveries at 90 ports over the previous 12 months, although the 13 leading ports accounted for 77.5% of recorded quantities. Singapore alone represented more than a quarter. Hydrogen, meanwhile, remains largely confined to demonstration projects and short-sea applications. The report also underscores the distinction between making alternative fuels available and ensuring they deliver meaningful emissions reductions. As gCaptain recently examined , LNG’s rapid adoption has brought increased scrutiny of methane slip, the unburned methane released from ship engines, particularly as European emissions regulations place greater financial consequences on greenhouse gas performance. The climate benefits of methanol and other emerging fuels likewise depend heavily on how they are produced, making the availability of genuinely low-carbon fuel supplies another challenge beyond bunkering infrastructure. For ports, LR says the next phase of the transition will depend on targeted investment, regulatory readiness and closer coordination with shipping companies and fuel suppliers. Berth-specific risk assessments, licensing, emergency response capabilities and workforce training will be essential to moving alternative fuels from trials into routine commercial operations. “For ports, investment should follow credible demand rather than trying to prepare for every fuel at once,” Ul Haq said. “Named vessel programmes and green shipping corridors are also ways to reduce infrastructure risk, alongside early investment in safety frameworks, licensing, emergency preparedness and workforce skills.” The central message for shipowners is that ordering a vessel capable of burning an alternative fuel is only part of the transition. Ensuring that fuel will be available, affordable and commercially viable along the ship’s intended trading routes is becoming just as important. articles.title: Céline Mortier elected new President of WISTA International

articles.body: WISTA International has elected Céline Mortier as its new President, succeeding Elpi Petraki, who completed four years in the role. The appointment took place during the WISTA International Annual General Meeting and Conference in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, from 28 to 30 October 2026. Céline Mortier, WISTA International President Mortier previously served as President of WISTA Belgium and is CEO of maritime services provider Bogerd Martin. She takes over the international association’s leadership following Petraki’s two consecutive terms. “Our greatest strength lies in the knowledge, experience and connections within our global network,” said Céline Mortier, President of WISTA International. She also highlighted the importance of strengthening cooperation between national associations and attracting younger professionals to the maritime industry. WISTA expands its international network During the AGM, WISTA International announced the addition of four new National WISTA Associations in the Bahamas, Egypt, Montenegro and the Philippines. As a result, the organisation now has 64 national associations and more than 6,500 members worldwide. The association also appointed Maryana Stober, Diruni Chanmugam and Amsha Gengan to its Executive Committee. They succeed Jemilat Mahamah, Dafne Anghelidis and Raimah Chowdhury. Meanwhile, outgoing President Elpi Petraki reflected on the importance of international cooperation and leadership development across the maritime industry. Petraki had previously secured a second term as WISTA International President in 2024 . The Kuala Lumpur conference brought together more than 250 professionals from the maritime, logistics and trading sectors. Discussions focused on regional cooperation, maritime security, sustainability and workforce development. International Maritime Organization Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez also addressed participants through a video message, highlighting initiatives to strengthen women’s participation in the maritime sector. The conference concluded with discussions on career development and workplace culture for women working at sea. WISTA International’s next AGM and Conference will take place in Brazil from 27 to 29 October 2027.

Photo courtesy Hanwha Philly Shipyard Hanwha Philly Shipyard has named shipbuilding veteran Hyuk Kim as its new president, effective November 2, as the Philadelphia yard moves ahead with plans to expand into U.S. Navy shipbuilding while maintaining its commercial operations. Kim, who brings more than 25 years of naval and commercial shipbuilding experience, succeeds David Kim, who helped oversee Hanwha’s acquisition of the shipyard in 2024 and a near doubling of its workforce since then. The leadership change comes amid a broader restructuring announced last week that will place the shipyard under the control of Hanwha Defense USA (HDUSA), the U.S. subsidiary of Hanwha Aerospace. Kim will report directly to retired Rear Adm. Tom Anderson, HDUSA’s president of U.S. shipbuilding, who oversees the company’s American shipbuilding operations. The appointment follows a series of major developments at the yard, including last week’s selection of HDUSA to build a $269 million Medium Landing Ship for the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps. The agreement with TOTE Services covers one vessel, with options for three additional ships. In July, the shipyard was also awarded a contract to build a Missile Range Instrumentation Vessel for the Missile Defense Agency, marking its first new-construction contract under Hanwha ownership. “Hanwha’s upgrades and investments in Philly Shipyard are enabling the yard to now build for the federal government as well as commercial ships, bringing the Philadelphia waterfront back to its roots as a key part of the Arsenal of Democracy,” Anderson said. He pointed to Hyuk Kim’s experience at Hanwha Ocean and its predecessor, Daewoo Shipbuilding & Marine Engineering, where he held senior positions. Hanwha Ocean’s flagship South Korean shipyard produces between 35 and 45 commercial and naval vessels annually, according to the company. “By building on the strong foundation established in the months since Hanwha acquired the yard, we will focus on strengthening operational excellence, expanding shipbuilding capacity, and developing the workforce needed to support both commercial and naval programs,” Kim said. Hanwha acquired the Philadelphia shipyard in December 2024 and has since outlined ambitious plans to modernize its facilities, expand production capacity and bring South Korean shipbuilding expertise to the United States. The transition into defense shipbuilding represents a significant shift for a facility that has long been one of America’s most important commercial shipyards. According to Hanwha, the yard has delivered approximately half of all large oceangoing Jones Act commercial vessels built in the United States since 2000. The expansion also raises an important question for the U.S. maritime industry: whether Hanwha can substantially increase naval production while continuing to serve the country’s commercial shipbuilding needs. Hanwha has maintained that its goal is to develop the Philadelphia facility into a dual-use shipyard capable of supporting both markets. The appointment of a new president with extensive experience in high-volume shipbuilding marks another step toward that goal. articles.title: When the ship pays back before the owner does
articles.summary: Fuel-saving retrofits can pay for themselves long before the shipowner who funded them sees a return. A new BIMCO contract seeks to resolve shipping’s longstanding divide between who pays for efficiency and who pockets the savings. Alex Byelyavtsev reports. DNV’s Maritime Forecast to 2050 has a 5,000 teu case: bow...
articles.body: Contributions Finance and Insurance Operations When the ship pays back before the owner does Splash November 3, 2026 0 312 3 minutes read Fuel-saving retrofits can pay for themselves long before the shipowner who funded them sees a return. A new BIMCO contract seeks to resolve shipping’s longstanding divide between who pays for efficiency and who pockets the savings. Alex Byelyavtsev reports. DNV’s Maritime Forecast to 2050 has a 5,000 teu case: bow modification, propeller retrofit and propeller boss cap fin. About 16% fuel saving. Payback around one to four years, depending on fuel price. Industry coverage puts the package at about $2.35m. That calculation belongs to the ship. It does not say who receives the saving. On time charter the owner owns the vessel. The charterer typically buys the bunkers. If the owner pays to burn less, the immediate fuel saving shows up first in the charterer’s accounts. If the charterer pays, the steel stays on someone else’s ship when the fixture ends. Take an illustrative case, not DNV’s discounted model. Assume 10,000 tonnes a year at $600 a tonne and a 16% cut. The saving is $960,000 a year. Against $2.35m of kit, the project’s simple payback is about 2.45 years. If the owner funds the whole amount and keeps half of that saving, the owner’s simple payback stretches to about 4.9 years. On a three-year charter, the retrofit would have generated $2.88m in fuel savings, $530,000 more than its initial cost. Yet the owner would have recovered only $1.44m, leaving $910,000 still unrecovered when the fixture ended. The ship can reach payback before the investor does. Same steel. Same fuel. Different payback. The 50/50 split is an assumption, not a BIMCO default. The sums ignore discounting, finance, off-hire, maintenance, residual value and any regulatory credit. The hardware usually stays with the owner. Cash can still arrive later than the invoice. Maersk described, in October 2025, a programme across about 200 time-chartered ships and 50 owners: more than 1,500 projects done, about 1,000 more aimed at 2027. The investment cost, it said, is split with the vessel owners. Many of those ships were designed for higher speeds. The schedules slowed. The propeller and the bow often did not. The charterer gets lower fuel costs and lower emissions. The owner gets a modernised asset. DP World Shipping Solutions and MPC Container Ships tested a more explicit version of the same bargain. On an MPC-owned vessel chartered by DP World, they jointly invested in energy-efficiency upgrades and amended the charterparty to share both installation costs and the resulting fuel-saving benefits. Vessel Performance Solutions monitored the performance improvements. The contract created a place for both. To share a performance benefit, someone has to say how much was saved. Last year’s 10,000 tonnes and this year’s 8,500 is not the proof. Speed, draft, weather, hull and profile all move the burn. The number that has to be agreed is a counterfactual: what this ship would have consumed if nothing had been fitted. BIMCO’s form even contemplates that a fuel-saving device may produce additional fuel consumption rather than a saving. That is why the contract needs a baseline, an assessment method and, where agreed, an independent assessor. On October 8 2026, BIMCO’s Documentary Committee adopted the Energy Saving Device Retrofit Addendum 2026. BIMCO’s reason is the time-charter split: the party that funds the retrofit may not take the main operational benefit. The form lets parties allocate cost, time implications and benefits. It does not prescribe one commercial model. Time is not a footnote. A ship can sit in the yard with hire running while the propeller comes off. The steel invoice has started. The bunker saving has not. The benefit does not stop at the bunker bill. Under BIMCO’s ETS clause for time charter, the charterer provides and pays for the allowances corresponding to the vessel’s emissions during the charter period. Burn less fuel in EU ETS scope and the charterer can need fewer allowances as well. The new retrofit addendum goes further: it lets the parties allocate environmental benefits separately from the operational ones. The same piece of equipment can therefore create value in more than one account. None of this means time charter stops investment. In July 2026, Seaspan and Maersk described about $75m in completed and planned fleet-upgrade investment across 18 vessels on long-term charter, including a major retrofit package for four 13,000 teu ships. The money can move. The question is on what terms. In March 2026, the Mærsk Mc-Kinney Møller Center published procedures for measuring retrofit savings. In June, it followed with a framework for sharing costs and benefits between owners and charterers. In October, BIMCO gave that bargain a standard contractual form. Shipping already knows how to save some of the fuel. The harder question has been who gets the saving. articles.body: DP World’s Shipping Solutions AMEA business will launch the China Africa Link, a new weekly service designed to strengthen maritime connectivity between the Far East and the growing markets of East and Southern Africa. The service is scheduled to commence in late November 2026 and will give customers greater choice, enhanced market access and more resilient supply chains. The rotation calls at Shanghai, Ningbo and Nansha in China, followed by Port Klang Westport in Malaysia, Dar es Salaam in Tanzania, Maputo in Mozambique and Singapore, before returning to Shanghai. It will carry machinery, electronics, construction materials and automotive components from China, alongside African exports such as agricultural products, minerals and other commodities. The service is presented as a practical example of DP World Marine Services’ Connected Trade Corridors approach, which brings together maritime solutions, ports and inland transport to build more integrated and flexible trade networks. It also complements DP World’s investments in African trade infrastructure, including a US$ 165 million expansion of the Maputo container terminal intended to more than double its handling capacity, and a commitment of more than US$ 500 million to modernise the Port of Dar es Salaam. Ganesh Raj, Global COO of Marine Services at DP World, said that as global trade changes, customers need more than shipping capacity: they need reliable connections, greater choice and the flexibility to adapt. He described the new service as bringing the Connected Trade Corridors approach to life by creating smarter, more flexible shipping networks that help keep cargo moving and support the continued growth of South–South trade.
