articles.title: How Potable Water Quality Impacts Crew Health & Safety
articles.summary: Dozens of miles offshore in the Gulf of Mexico, a worker turns on a shower after a 12-hour shift. The water flows clear and strong, unremarkable in every way, just as...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Underwater splash with bubbles. Dozens of miles offshore in the Gulf of Mexico, a worker turns on a shower after a 12-hour shift. The water flows clear and strong, unremarkable in every way, just as it should be. However, that water represents a complex network of filtration, disinfection, storage, and monitoring that provides crew members with the clean water they need to live and work at sea for weeks at a time. Potable water systems on offshore platforms and maritime vessels are critical infrastructure that crews rely on every single day, yet they operate largely out of sight and out of mind. These systems must transport thousands of gallons of water daily, maintain quality through unpredictable conditions, and do so in an environment where contamination can spread rapidly through confined quarters. When water filtration and transportation systems fail, they place workers at risk of contracting deadly waterborne illnesses. Water tanks and systems themselves may also present hazards related to entrapment, toxic exposure, and asphyxiation. Understanding these dangers and the measures in place to prevent them is critical to maritime worker safety. Offshore platforms and vessels obtain potable water through two primary methods: bunkering from shore-based supplies or producing it onboard through desalination. Bunkering involves loading potable water from land-based sources onto the rig or vessel through specialized hoses and connections. Supply vessels transport water from port facilities to offshore installations, where it’s transferred into onboard storage tanks. Hoses used for potable water must be dedicated solely for that purpose, properly capped when not in use, and disinfected if they’ve been idle for more than 14 days. Water samples must be taken and tested before bunkering begins. Contamination risks are present when hoses are not flushed properly or when connections are not sealed correctly. Water that passed quality standards on shore might deteriorate during transport and storage if not appropriately managed. Desalination through reverse osmosis (RO) offers a more sustainable alternative by allowing platforms and vessels to produce their own freshwater from seawater, which is abundant all around them. The technology works by forcing seawater through membranes under high pressure. The membranes allow water molecules to pass through while blocking dissolved salts, minerals, bacteria, and viruses. The desalination process begins with seawater intake, often drawn from about 20 to 30 feet below the surface to avoid surface contaminants. Raw seawater passes through pre-treatment systems to remove larger particles, sediment, and organic matter that could damage the delicate membranes. High-pressure pumps then force the pre-treated water through the membranes. Fresh water emerges on one side; concentrated brine is discharged back to the sea on the other. Modern offshore RO systems can produce anywhere from a few hundred to tens of thousands of gallons of fresh water every day, depending on the size of the installation and crew. The technology is efficient, consuming far less energy than older thermal distillation methods, but the systems are complex and must be monitored. Performance and water quality can all be affected by membrane fouling, mineral buildup, or biological growth. Potable water must be stored and distributed safely to reach crew quarters, galleys, and other points of use. This is where many problems begin. Potable water storage tanks on offshore installations and vessels may range from a few thousand to tens of thousands of gallons in capacity. These tanks must be constructed from materials approved for potable water use, with coatings that resist corrosion and don’t leach contaminants. Steel tanks are common, but they present a significant challenge: rust. As steel oxidizes, it consumes oxygen from the water and creates conditions favorable for bacterial growth, including Legionella . Distribution piping carries water from storage tanks to taps, showers, and other fixtures throughout the installation or vessel. The type of piping material makes a considerable difference in water quality. Traditional steel piping corrodes over time. Newer systems use stainless steel, copper, or plastic piping to minimize these issues, but older platforms often retain decades-old steel pipe that requires constant attention and maintenance. Water temperature within the distribution system is another key factor in preventing the growth of bacteria. The CDC recommends storing hot water at temperatures above 140°F and storing and circulating cold water at temperatures below 77°F, although Legionella can grow at temperatures as low as 68°F. Hot water systems that don’t maintain sufficiently high temperatures and cold water systems that aren’t kept adequately cool both create ideal conditions for bacterial growth. Disinfection through chlorination is the primary defense against waterborne pathogens, and offshore installations typically maintain a chlorine level of 0.2 to 0.5 milligrams per liter. But maintaining proper chlorine levels throughout a complex distribution system, especially one with dead legs or infrequently used fixtures, requires careful monitoring. Legionella pneumophila represents the most significant waterborne health threat to offshore and maritime workers. This organism causes Legionnaires’ disease, a severe form of pneumonia that kills approximately 10% of those infected and can be particularly dangerous for workers over 50, smokers, or those with compromised immune systems. Legionella occurs naturally in freshwater environments but becomes a health hazard when it multiplies in man-made water systems. When contaminated water is aerosolized (turned into a fine spray or mist) through showers, cooling towers, or other spray-producing devices, workers can inhale the bacteria-laden droplets and become infected. The risk on maritime vessels is substantial when potable water systems are not properly monitored and maintained. A 2018 study examining water samples from 360 non-passenger merchant vessels docked at UK ports found that 58% tested positive for Legionella , with 27% of samples showing levels above the upper action limit (when immediate remediation is required). According to the CDC, Legionnaires’ disease has an incubation period of 2 to 14 days. Symptoms include fever, cough, shortness of breath, muscle aches, and headaches. The disease doesn’t spread from person to person, but a single contaminated water system can simultaneously sicken multiple workers. For offshore and maritime workers, where medical evacuation may take time and onboard medical facilities are limited, a Legionnaires’ outbreak can quickly become life-threatening. Beyond Legionella , other waterborne pathogens pose risks. Coliform bacteria, like E. coli , indicate fecal contamination and can cause gastroenteritis. While cruise ship norovirus outbreaks make headlines, similar gastrointestinal illnesses can devastate offshore crews, where workers live in close quarters and share common facilities. The difference is that vessels and offshore installations may be miles from shore, with limited medical facilities and personnel on board to manage an outbreak. The framework governing potable water quality for seamen and offshore workers involves multiple federal agencies and international standards. The U.S. Coast Guard has primary responsibility for vessel sanitation and potable water quality on ships under its jurisdiction. The Coast Guard enforces standards for water production, storage, and distribution systems aboard vessels and conducts inspections to verify compliance with federal sanitation requirements. The Maritime Labour Convention (MLC) 2006 , which entered into force in 2013, established international standards for potable water on ships. Regulation 3.2 requires that vessels provide adequate supplies of safe drinking water for crew consumption, food preparation, and personal hygiene. The convention mandates that water must be of appropriate quality and quantity, and itmust not cause immediate or long-term harm to those using it. For offshore installations in federal waters, oversight is less centralized. While BSEE regulates offshore safety and environmental protection, potable water quality on fixed platforms falls into a regulatory gray area with less clear federal oversight compared to vessels. Industry guidelines and company safety management systems must fill this gap. Potable water systems must be correctly (and continually) monitored and controlled to ensure the safety of the offshore crews and seamen who rely on them. This includes: • Mandatory Water Quality Testing & Transparency : Potable water should be tested regularly for the presence of Legionella, coliform bacteria, chemicals, and other contaminants. Testing cannot wait until problems are already evident. Proactive monitoring keeps water quality safe and consistent. • System Design & Maintenance : Older installations with aging steel piping and storage tanks should be systematically upgraded with materials that resist corrosion and bacterial colonization. Dead-end sections and infrequently used taps or showers must be flushed regularly. Water temperatures must be kept at safe levels to inhibit bacterial growth. • Training & Education : All workers should receive training on waterborne illness risks, proper hygiene practices, and how to report water quality concerns. • Water Safety Plans : Every offshore installation and vessel should have a comprehensive, regularly updated Water Safety Plan that identifies all potential contamination points, establishes monitoring procedures, and defines clear protocols for responding to water quality issues. The technology exists to provide safe, high-quality potable water to offshore workers. Reverse osmosis systems can produce fresh water from seawater with efficiency and reliability. Modern materials resist corrosion and bacterial growth. Monitoring equipment can detect contamination before it causes illness. What’s often missing is the commitment to implement these systems properly and maintain them rigorously over time. For offshore workers, potable water isn’t just a convenience or a luxury. It’s a necessity that directly impacts their health, safety, and ability to perform demanding work in an already challenging environment. ### Arnold & Itkin has been fighting for injured maritime workers since 2004, securing billions of dollars in verdicts and settlements, including some of the largest in U.S. history. articles.title: Port of Gdańsk recorded increased cargo handling
articles.summary: The Port of Gdańsk handled 65.2 million tonnes of cargo between January and September 2026, compared with 59.1 million tonnes in the same period of 2025, an increase of more than 10%. articles.body: The Port of Gdańsk handled 65.2 million tonnes of cargo between January and September 2026, compared with 59.1 million tonnes in the same period of 2025, an increase of more than 10%. General cargo, and containerised cargo in particular, accounted for the largest share of the growth. General cargo totalled 23.5 million tonnes, 3.6 million tonnes or 18 per cent more than a year earlier. Containerised cargo reached 21.1 million tonnes, up 17.6%, while container throughput rose 21% from just over 2 million to nearly 2.5 million TEUs. Coal handling grew 36 per cent to 6.7 million tonnes, an additional 1.8 million tonnes, and grain rose 33 per cent to 2.1 million tonnes, more than half a million tonnes above the previous year. The only category to decline was other bulk cargo, which fell 1.5 per cent to 2.8 million tonnes. Liquid fuels remain the largest cargo group, representing around 45% of all cargo with 29.4 million tonnes, a level similar to the previous year. General cargo accounts for over 36% volumes and coal for around 10%. Dorota Pyć, President of the Management Board of the Port of Gdańsk, attributed the result to favourable conditions in key market segments, rising containerised volumes and stable fuel handling, which confirms the port’s importance for Poland’s energy security. She said the continued development of infrastructure and operational capacity remains the priority, so that the port can respond flexibly to changing market conditions and strengthen its position within international supply chains as the leading port of the Baltic Sea region.

November 2, 2026 © Adobe Stock/StreetOnCamara Six months after leaving OPEC, the United Arab Emirates on Monday began hosting ADIPEC, one of the world's largest energy conferences, where it told an audience of industry executives it had increased oil exports in spite of the Iran war. The UAE was for 59 years a pivotal member of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries. It said in April it would leave the group, weeks into the US-Israeli war with Iran. The war, which began at the end of February, has led to severe disruption of energy supplies and has driven oil prices higher. UAE energy minister Suhail al-Mazrouei said at ADIPEC on Monday his country's exports on occasions had been better than before the war without giving precise details. The UAE will protect its energy infrastructure and invest in new export routes, he told ADIPEC. The conference continues in Abu Dhabi until Thursday. OPEC figures compiled from secondary sources support the comments. In September, the UAE pumped 3.917 million barrels per day of crude, up 15% from February, the figures show. The September figure is 470,000 bpd more than the OPEC+ quota that would have applied to the UAE in May had it not left OPEC and the wider OPEC+ as of May 1. The remaining regional members of OPEC+, excluding Oman, pumped below theirs. IEA FIGURES PUT UAE OUTPUT HIGHER The International Energy Agency has assessed UAE output higher still. It said that for September it expected UAE production to have been 4.4 million bpd. Taking crude oil, condensate and other liquids into account, the UAE pumped a record 5.3 million bpd in September, the IEA said last month. The Abu Dhabi National Oil Company disputes the data quoted by Reuters. Reuters sought comment from the state oil company on the OPEC and IEA output figures, on export data showing UAE shipments were higher than those of Saudi Arabia in August, and on the suggestion that the UAE had benefited from leaving OPEC. "We have advised Reuters that the data in this story is wrong and this report is inaccurate," a spokesperson for ADNOC said. ADNOC did not specify what was inaccurate in the data or report, nor did it provide alternative data. The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and authorities from Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil exporter and leading member of OPEC, did not reply to a request for comment. UAE WELL-PLACED TO MEET DEMAND FOR OIL International oil prices have reached multiyear highs as the disruption caused by the Iran war has reduced supplies. They fell on Monday after talks between Iranian and Qatari officials lifted expectations of peace talks and a day after OPEC+ left output targets steady. Analysts say overall supplies are tight, especially of some refined products, and that strategic inventories governments have drawn upon need to be refilled. Two people with knowledge of oil policy in the UAE said being freed from OPEC production constraints had put the UAE in a good position to meet demand. Western energy analysts also said the UAE had felt able to act as boldly as required. "The UAE has come out ahead and leaving OPEC clearly helped," Rystad Energy analyst Rahul Choudhary said, referring to how the country fared relative to regional countries on navigating the war. Abu Dhabi rapidly expanded ship-to-ship transfers to move crude beyond the Strait of Hormuz. "The UAE has been producing above pre-war levels since June," said Richard Bronze of Energy Aspects. "I see this mainly as a result of it being willing and able to take risks to restart exports earlier than other regional producers rather than a function of the decision to leave OPEC." (Reuters)

articles.title: Oil Prices Drop 7% as Iran, Qatar Open to Peace Talks
articles.summary: Oil prices fell more than 7% on Monday as talks between Iranian and Qatari officials lifted hopes for an end to the US-Israeli war with Iran and stabilization of Middle East crude supply.Iran's president said the supreme leader had granted the government "certain authorities" regarding peace talks.
articles.body: Oil Prices Drop 7% as Iran, Qatar Open to Peace Talks Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 2, 2026 © Adobe Stock/ le Oil prices fell more than 7% on Monday as talks between Iranian and Qatari officials lifted hopes for an end to the US-Israeli war with Iran and stabilization of Middle East crude supply. Iran's president said the supreme leader had granted the government "certain authorities" regarding peace talks. The country's negotiators held days of talks with Qatari mediators aimed at ending the war. A draft proposal is being circulated with a follow-up meeting possible, an official briefed on the talks said. Brent crude futures fell $8.47, or 7.47%, to $104.96 a barrel by 12:24 p.m. EST (1724 GMT). US West Texas Intermediate crude was down $7.50, or 7.2%, at $96.62. The session low for Brent was $104.49 and for WTI it was $96.44, with analysts citing hopes for a diplomatic breakthrough after Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei had granted the government certain authorities for peace talks. Pezeshkian added Tehran "will try to resolve the problem with dialogue", without elaborating, according to state media. Signs of progress in US-Iran talks pushed oil prices lower, Raymond James analyst Pavel Molchanov said, noting, however, that skepticism is warranted after many "false dawns” over the past several months. Brent ended October at its highest in six months on concerns that the Middle East conflict could escalate again after Tuesday's US midterm elections. "The oil market is still reacting with extreme sensitivity to every headline out of the Middle East," UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo said. "While fears of an imminent escalation pushed prices up last week, they have dropped sharply at the start of this week as diplomatic talks between the US and Iran continue," he added. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that the purpose of the talks was to continue consultations with the Qatari mediators, adding that Tehran was prepared for "both defence and diplomacy". The talks followed a recent increase in attacks on oil tankers passing the Strait of Hormuz, though there have also been signs of shipments rising from some major exporters. Saudi Arabia's crude exports increased in Octoberfrom September, two of three ship-tracking companies said, despite attacks by Iran-aligned Yemeni Houthis on its energy infrastructure. The outbreak of the Iran war at the end of February has depleted oil stocks. The world has drained nearly 1 billion barrels from inventories since the war disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, said Sultan Al Jaber, chief executive of ADNOC, Abu Dhabi's state-owned oil company. Oil could rise further, some analysts said. Goldman Sachs on Sunday, citing elevated supply, and said Brent could jump to $140 in 2027 if Gulf oil output remains 3.5 million barrels per day below its 2025 average. "Intensified shipping attacks, damage to oil infrastructure, and a more persistent risk premium remain the key triggers of potential upside," the bank said in a report. (Reuters)

articles.title: Seven Migrants Die Offshore Canary Islands
articles.summary: At least seven migrants died off Spain's Canary Islands while more than 380 people were rescued on Monday, the country's maritime rescue services said.Two deceased people were found aboard a migrant boat when the coast guard rescued 132 people on Monday, 150 km (94 miles) off Lanzarote.
articles.body: Seven Migrants Die Offshore Canary Islands Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 2, 2026 © Adobe Stock/ Peter Hermes Furian At least seven migrants died off Spain's Canary Islands while more than 380 people were rescued on Monday, the country's maritime rescue services said. Two deceased people were found aboard a migrant boat when the coast guard rescued 132 people on Monday, 150 km (94 miles) off Lanzarote. During the same journey, five other migrants had died and been thrown into the sea, authorities added. Another 250 migrants were rescued by coast guard boats off Lanzarote and the Canary Island of El Hierro earlier on Monday, authorities said. On Sunday, 107 migrants were rescued off El Hierro, according to authorities. "The worst forecasts are coming true. The Atlantic route is once again claiming lives, this time off the coast of Lanzarote. Behind each one is a life, a story, and a family," Canary Islands President Fernando Clavijo said in a message on X. The Atlantic route from West Africa to the Canary Islands is one of the world's deadliest migration crossings. Thousands of migrants attempt the journey each year in overcrowded boats, seeking to reach Spanish territory despite rough seas, strong currents and long distances. Arrivals tend to pick up in the autumn months, when sea conditions along the route are generally calmer and more favorable for crossings. Migrant arrivals have declined so far this year compared with the same period in 2025, but crossings increased sharply in October, putting additional pressure on reception and emergency services on some of the Canary Islands, particularly the smaller and less densely populated ones. Migrant arrivals in the archipelago have fallen 18% year on year to 11,527 people, according to the office of the Spanish government's representative in the Canary Islands. (Reuters)

Join the leading maritime news network Port of Long Beach A broad coalition of maritime, agricultural, manufacturing, retail and logistics organizations is urging the Trump administration to permanently suspend U.S. port fees targeting China-linked vessels, warning that reinstating the charges would raise costs for American businesses, hurt exporters and disrupt global supply chains. In an October 30 letter to U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer , the coalition welcomed the proposed two-month extension of the Section 301 vessel fee suspension through January 9, 2027, but called on Washington to go further and eliminate the charges permanently. Signatories include the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, National Association of Manufacturers, National Retail Federation, American Farm Bureau Federation, American Association of Port Authorities, International Chamber of Shipping and World Shipping Council, along with hundreds of other trade associations representing businesses that depend on ocean transportation. The groups argue that reinstating the fees would add another layer of costs to supply chains already struggling with elevated freight rates, equipment availability challenges and uncertainty in global trade. Because Chinese-built ships account for a significant share of global shipping capacity, the coalition warned that the impact would extend well beyond Chinese shipping companies, affecting vessel deployments and transportation costs for American importers and exporters. The letter also raised concerns about provisions targeting foreign-built roll-on/roll-off vessels, which could affect shipping companies from U.S. allied nations and disrupt transportation services relied upon by American manufacturers. For importers, the fees could mean higher transportation surcharges and increased prices for consumer goods and industrial inputs. For exporters, including agricultural producers and manufacturers, the charges could make American products less competitive in overseas markets. The coalition also challenged the idea that port fees would meaningfully rebuild America’s struggling commercial shipbuilding industry. The groups argued that the underlying challenges behind China’s dominance, including limited U.S. shipbuilding capacity, workforce shortages and a lack of competitive alternatives, remain unresolved. Instead, they called for a dedicated long-term shipbuilding strategy backed by sustained investment and commitments from both the public and private sectors. The World Shipping Council separately submitted comments to USTR , supporting efforts to revitalize American shipbuilding but arguing that sustained legislative measures, government support and workforce development would be more effective than sweeping vessel fees. The latest industry appeal follows the Trump administration’s October 23 proposal to extend the suspension through January 9, 2027, as Washington and Beijing continue negotiations over China’s dominance of the maritime, logistics and shipbuilding sectors. The fees were originally imposed in October 2025 before being suspended the following month under a broader U.S.-China trade agreement. The existing suspension is scheduled to expire November 9 unless the proposed extension takes effect. The push for a permanent suspension comes amid competing pressure from lawmakers and maritime labor unions, which argue that the fees are necessary to counter China’s state-supported shipbuilding industry and encourage investment in American shipyards. Senators Mark Kelly and Elizabeth Warren have previously urged the administration to reinstate the charges, warning that the suspension undermines efforts to rebuild U.S. commercial shipbuilding capacity. articles.summary: Contacts between Iran and the United States to end their eight-month war are continuing, Tehran said on Monday, after days of Iranian talks with Qatari mediators ended with altered proposals but no breakthrough.

REUTERS/Stringer DUBAI, Nov 2 (Reuters) – Contacts between Iran and the United States to end their eight-month war are continuing, Tehran said on Monday, after days of Iranian talks with Qatari mediators ended with altered proposals but no breakthrough. “Consultations through mediators are very intensive. We have presented our conditions and proposals and everything depends on the political rationality of Washington,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said in comments carried by state media outlet IRNA. Amid fears the conflict could reignite after Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States, China and Russia both spoke out on Monday against the possibility of renewed military action in a war that has hit the global economy. IRANIAN SOURCES THINK US ATTACK MORE LIKELY THAN DEAL While oil prices fell nearly 4% on Monday on hopes that the latest round of mediation could lead to a diplomatic solution to the crisis, Iranian sources said they believed a new US attack was still more likely than a deal. Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said the plan Iran had submitted in September to end the war remained the focus of discussions, but he confirmed comments attributed to Araqchi on Saturday that the proposal could be shortened. “The basis of dialog and talks between Iran and the US via mediators is still Iran’s seven-step proposal, which is now condensed, making it possible to implement it within two days,” he said. US President Donald Trump rejected the seven-step proposal in September. The plan would call for the US to end its blockade on Iranian ports, Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz waterway, a US waiver on Iranian oil sales, the cancellation of new sanctions on Iran and then talks on other issues. Baghaei reiterated that condensing the plan would not change Iran’s underlying stance that a return to talks on the country’s nuclear program could only happen after it verified that all its conditions were met. Asked whether the possibility of transferring Iran’s highly enriched uranium stockpile to another country was raised in the talks, and whether Iran might agree to that, he said no. An official briefed on the talks said Iran’s negotiators had left on Sunday but not because of any problems in the talks, and added that a draft proposal was being circulated without elaborating. RUSSIAN AND CHINESE CONCERNS The war, which the US and Israel launched suddenly on February 28, has led to Iran’s closure of the key Strait of Hormuz waterway, the US blockade on Iranian ports, repeated bouts of Iranian drone and missile fire on Gulf states and renewed conflict in Yemen. Trump has repeatedly said there would be no new attack on Iran before Tuesday’s midterm elections. Iran has said it will respond to any resumed attack aggressively with plans to strike targets both within and outside the Middle East. China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi said on Monday that all parties to the conflict should focus on political solutions rather than resorting to arms again, after a meeting with senior Iranian security official Ali Bagheri Kani in Beijing. China, a major customer for Gulf energy products, is engaging more actively in Middle East diplomacy this week, hosting Oman’s Sultan Haitham bin Tariq al-Said, whose country flanks the southern side of the Strait of Hormuz. Wang also met Saudi Arabia’s national security advisor Musaed bin Mohammed al-Aiban in Beijing on Monday, China’s Foreign Ministry said, adding that all sides should work to safeguard regional energy and shipping lane security. In Moscow, the Russian Foreign Ministry said reports of new military action against Iran were a cause for extreme concern and called for increased diplomatic efforts. Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke by phone with Iran’s top security official Mohsen Rezaei on Monday, Iranian state media reported. Underscoring the risks to global energy supply, a Qatari liquefied natural gas (LNG) tanker was struck in the Gulf by unidentified objects on Friday, its operator Nakilat said on Sunday. While attacks on oil tankers in the Gulf and Red Sea have been common during the conflict, attacks on LNG carriers have been rare, with the last reported incident with a Qatari tanker happening in early July. articles.summary: (Bloomberg) — Pakistan negotiated with Iran to secure safe passage for liquefied natural gas carrier Al Mayeda before the ship was attacked near the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, according...

Join the leading maritime news network Oleksandr Kalinichenko / Shutterstock (Bloomberg) — Pakistan negotiated with Iran to secure safe passage for liquefied natural gas carrier Al Mayeda before the ship was attacked near the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter. The Marshall Islands-flagged vessel was sailing toward the waterway loaded with LNG from Qatar when it came under fire, the people said, asking not to be named as they are not authorized to speak to the media. Just hours earlier, Iranian authorities were understood to have provided a green light, they added. The ship subsequently turned around and headed into the Persian Gulf, according to ship-tracking data. “Qatar reserves its right to take all necessary measures, in accordance with international law and the UN Charter, to protect its assets and safeguard its vessels and their crews,” the Qatari Foreign Ministry said in a statement on Sunday, adding that authorities are investigating the incident and those responsible. Indian Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal wrote on X that the ship had been targeted in a projectile attack. He said all 25 crew members, including six Indian nationals, were safe but didn’t provide further details. Qatar Gas Transport Company Ltd., known as Nakilat, said on Sunday that the carrier remained operational and was being assessed. New Wave of Attacks Hits Tankers and LNG Carrier in Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf It wasn’t immediately clear why the tanker came under fire or whether it would still attempt to reach its destination. Pakistan, apparently benefiting from its ties with Iran and its role as mediator, has communicated with Iranian authorities over the safety of several other shipments of Qatari LNG over the past month, all of which crossed successfully into the Gulf of Oman. The incident underscores the continued risk for vessels navigating around Hormuz and poses a fresh challenge for Pakistan, which has grappled for months with an energy shortfall as a result of upheaval in the Middle East. Without the LNG shipment, Pakistan could be forced to turn to the spot market, where prices are more than three times pre-war levels. Pakistan’s petroleum ministry, QatarEnergy and Iran’s foreign ministry didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. LNG flows through Hormuz held steady in October at about 30% of pre-war levels. Qatar has been sending LNG through the waterway consistently since September, including on older vessels that can help reduce the additional insurance costs associated with the risky voyages. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.summary: The Liguria Region, working with Lombardy and Piedmont, organised the two-day event “Connections Shaping the Future: North-Western Italy as an Integrated Network” in Genoa. articles.body: The Liguria Region, working with Lombardy and Piedmont, organised the two-day event “Connections Shaping the Future: North-Western Italy as an Integrated Network” in Genoa. Rail carries about 30% of overland freight at Savona-Vado and 12.5% at Genoa, and the aim is to lift Genoa’s share to at least 30%. The presidents of the three regions, Marco Bucci, Alberto Cirio and Attilio Fontana, attended, and Infrastructure and Transport Minister Matteo Salvini gave the closing address. President Matteo Paroli of the Western Ligurian Sea Port Authority said the ports of Genoa and Savona-Vado are the main maritime gateway for 80% of manufacturing firms in Northern Italy. They account for roughly 30 percent of Italy’s import VAT revenue and support 121,000 direct and indirect jobs. Paroli described the guiding vision as a port that generates wealth while minimising its impact on the surrounding urban area. Genoa’s new open-sea breakwater, an investment of about EUR 1.4 billion, will receive ultra-large vessels of up to 400 metres by providing direct access and a wide turning basin in the Sampierdarena Basin. Paroli stressed that such a project must sit within a wider logistics network, pointing to the forthcoming Terzo Valico high-speed, high-capacity rail line linking Genoa to Lombardy and the European hinterland. Last-mile rail projects now nearing completion will allow the ports to handle intermodal trains of up to 750 metres and 1,750 tonnes per train with a single locomotive, which he called essential for an economically viable and sustainable rail service. The authority has allocated about EUR 230 million to rail infrastructure at Genoa and Savona-Vado, covering IT upgrades, safety systems and electrification of intermodal areas. To help, the authority is exploring incentives for terminal operators and closer coordination among logistics providers, manufacturers and public bodies. It is also in talks with the Italian Customs Agency and other local authorities about extending operating hours, now 6 am to 6 pm, and is working with the road haulage sector to ease congestion. Paroli added that congestion at major Northern European hubs and falling water levels on Europe’s main rivers could further raise the role of Mediterranean ports in international supply chains.

articles.body: WMU Celebrates 2026 Graduates Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 2, 2026 © World Maritime University On October 31, the World Maritime University (WMU) celebrated the graduation of the Class of 2026. Representing a global community of maritime and oceans professionals, the graduates are equipped to apply their knowledge and expertise to the challenges facing the sector and contribute to a safer, more sustainable maritime and oceans future. This year’s ceremony brings WMU’s global alumni network to nearly 7,000 professionals across 173 countries and territories. Welcome remarks were delivered by WMU President, Professor Maximo Q. Mejia, Jr., who expressed gratitude to the families and friends of the graduates, WMU staff, donors, and partners for their contributions to the University and its mission. Addressing the graduates, he emphasized that, beyond the knowledge and skills reflected in their degrees, some of the greatest benefits of their time at WMU include the ability they have gained to collaborate across cultures and professional backgrounds. He encouraged the graduates to make use of the global network they have built at WMU, and to grow this network, continue learning, question assumptions and rethink established approaches as they carry the WMU spirit into their professional lives. Mr Arsenio Dominguez, Chancellor of WMU and Secretary-General of the International Maritime Organization (IMO), thanked the Government of Sweden, the City of Malmö and international donors for their continued support of the University. Acknowledging the challenges currently facing shipping, he urged graduates to see them as an opportunity to contribute to positive change. He encouraged them to share the knowledge and experience gained at WMU, remain lifelong learners, and support the development of others. Noting that he regularly encounters WMU graduates in his travels around the world, he highlighted the value of the University’s global network and encouraged graduates to maintain their WMU connections throughout their careers. In his address, Guest of Honour Mr Gerardo Borromeo, Chairperson of the WMU Executive Board and CEO of Philippine Transmarine Carriers, reflected on how WMU brings together maritime professionals from different cultures and countries, helping them discover how much they have in common and the importance of cooperation and understanding in an international industry. He challenged the graduates to consider what they would do differently as a result of their time at WMU, and to become leaders and ambassadors for an industry that moves the world but often remains invisible to it. He emphasized that a key aspect of leadership is creating opportunities for others to grow, preparing them to take the helm, and seeing what becomes possible when you give others a chance. On behalf of the City of Malmö, Ms. Anja Nordberg Sonesson, Vice President of the Malmö City Council, congratulated the graduates and expressed the City’s pride in hosting WMU. She highlighted the shared diversity of WMU, with graduates from 171 countries, and Malmö, whose residents represent 186 nations, noting how this diversity fosters relationships, mutual understanding and a foundation for peace. Photo: Carnival Cruise Line Orders for alternative-fueled ships are running 57% ahead of last year, with LNG-powered containerships and car carriers driving much of the growth, according to new figures from classification society DNV. Shipowners ordered 53 alternative-fueled vessels in October, bringing the year-to-date total to 364 vessels, according to DNV’s Alternative Fuels Insight (AFI) platform. The latest figures extend a rebound in contracting activity that began over the summer, following a relatively slow start to 2026. LNG remained the clear favorite in October, accounting for 30 new orders, including 18 containerships and 12 car carriers. Another 19 orders were recorded for LPG carriers, while four ammonia-fueled car carriers were added to DNV’s database. The ammonia orders represent another step toward commercial adoption of the emerging fuel, although the technology and supporting bunkering infrastructure remain in the early stages of development. LNG has accounted for 230 alternative-fuel vessel orders so far in 2026, representing approximately 63% of the total. Containerships lead the LNG segment with 134 orders, followed by car carriers with 75. Together, the two vessel types account for more than 90% of LNG-fueled newbuild orders this year. “October’s figures add to the strong activity we have seen in alternative-fuelled vessel ordering since the summer,” said Jason Stefanatos, Global Decarbonization Director at DNV Maritime. “Particularly notable is the continued concentration of LNG-fuelled orders in container ships and car carriers.” The figures follow an especially strong third quarter, when shipowners placed orders for 168 alternative-fueled vessels, the highest quarterly total in two years. September alone accounted for 69 orders, as gCaptain previously reported . Stefanatos pointed to LNG’s established supply chain and growing bunkering network as key advantages over competing fuels. “LNG’s continued prominence is also supported by the comparatively mature infrastructure and supply chain around the fuel,” he said. The ability to potentially transition to lower-carbon fuels in the future also gives shipowners flexibility when investing in vessels expected to remain in service for decades. Still, LNG’s growing popularity comes amid continued debate over its long-term environmental benefits, particularly the impact of methane emissions. While LNG can reduce certain air pollutants compared with conventional marine fuels, its overall climate performance depends on factors including methane leakage and engine emissions. For now, the latest ordering figures suggest shipowners are continuing to favor LNG’s commercial availability and established infrastructure over newer fuel technologies, even as the industry considers longer-term decarbonization options. REUTERS/Stringer A tanker was struck by two unidentified projectiles in the Persian Gulf late Sunday, marking the latest in a series of attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz that have left vessels damaged, triggered onboard fires and forced the evacuation of 25 seafarers. According to UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) , the latest attack occurred at 2347 UTC on November 1, approximately 72 nautical miles east of Ras Al Khafji, Saudi Arabia. The tanker was traveling southeast when two unidentified projectiles struck its port side. All crew members were accounted for, and no environmental damage was reported. UKMTO did not identify the vessel or provide details on the extent of the damage. The attack followed another incident earlier Sunday in the Strait of Hormuz, where the master of a merchant vessel reported receiving a Mayday call over VHF Channel 16 from another ship that had reportedly been struck by an unknown projectile. UKMTO issued Warning 191-26 for that incident, which occurred at 1509 UTC. The identity of the vessel, extent of damage and condition of its crew remain unknown. The two incidents add to a growing series of attacks that have increasingly threatened commercial shipping throughout the Arabian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz. The Royal Navy of Oman confirmed Friday that it had evacuated 25 crew members from the Panama-flagged tanker RITI after the vessel was attacked and caught fire near the Musandam Peninsula. The evacuation was carried out in coordination with Oman’s Maritime Security Centre, with the rescued seafarers receiving medical care. According to the Joint Maritime Information Center’s November 1 advisory , RITI was struck by an unidentified projectile on October 29 while transiting outbound through the Strait of Hormuz near Khasab, Oman. The strike caused a small fire and loss of propulsion. The advisory also identified another tanker, LOUISE 1 , that was attacked October 29 approximately 25 nautical miles northeast of Khasab. In that incident, a small boat reportedly approached the tanker and attached two explosive devices to its hull above the waterline. The resulting explosions caused an engine-room fire and temporarily disabled the vessel. The crew was reported safe, and the tanker subsequently continued its voyage. A third tanker, the VLCC ARZANAH , was also struck by an unidentified projectile while transiting outbound through the Strait of Hormuz on October 28. The vessel sustained damage, although its crew was reported safe. The violence has also extended deeper into the Arabian Gulf. Qatar’s state-owned LNG shipping company Nakilat confirmed that its LNG carrier AL MAYEDA was struck by unidentified objects while transiting the Gulf on October 30. JMIC identified the incident as an attack approximately 40 nautical miles south of Iran’s Lavan Island and reported that the strike caused a fire onboard. Nakilat said there were no injuries or environmental damage and that the vessel remained safe and operational. In a statement issued November 1 , Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs strongly condemned the attack, describing it as a serious threat to maritime navigation and global energy security. Qatar said it reserved the right to take necessary measures under international law to protect its ships and crews, while authorities investigate the circumstances and identify those responsible. The ministry also warned of the potential environmental consequences of targeting energy carriers, particularly for the Gulf’s marine environment and regional water security. In its latest advisory, JMIC maintained its SEVERE threat assessment for the Strait of Hormuz, warning that further deliberate attacks were highly likely. The center recorded 18 confirmed attacks in the Strait since October 6 as of its November 1 assessment, before the two latest UKMTO warnings were incorporated. JMIC also warned that Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps activity continued to include surveillance, UAV overflights, radio hailing and pressure on merchant vessels to use Iranian-controlled transit routes. Commercial traffic remains significantly below prewar levels. According to JMIC, 119 U.S.-facilitated transits were recorded between October 29 and 31, while approximately 490 vessels were waiting outside the Strait of Hormuz as of November 1. The latest attacks underscore the continuing risks facing merchant vessels even as U.S. naval forces coordinate shipping movements through the strategically important waterway. With tankers and LNG carriers now being targeted both inside the Strait and farther into the Arabian Gulf, the security threat extends beyond the narrow shipping corridor itself, raising further concerns for global energy supplies and regional maritime operations. articles.title: ONE expands container reuse services to Switzerland with Avantida
articles.summary: Ocean Network Express (ONE) has introduced container reuse services in Switzerland through its collaboration with Avantida, allowing transport operators to reuse import containers for export shipments. articles.body: Ocean Network Express (ONE) has introduced container reuse services in Switzerland through its collaboration with Avantida, allowing transport operators to reuse import containers for export shipments. The service aims to reduce unnecessary empty container movements and improve the efficiency of inland logistics operations. Under the arrangement, transport companies can reuse eligible import containers for export cargo instead of returning them to a depot before collecting another empty unit. This process, commonly known as a street turn, can help reduce additional truck journeys, waiting times and transport costs. Improving inland container operations Through Avantida’s container reuse solution, ONE customers in Switzerland can explore opportunities to connect import and export container movements more efficiently. The approach can simplify transport planning and reduce congestion associated with unnecessary empty container repositioning. In addition, fewer empty container movements could help lower fuel consumption and related CO₂ emissions. However, the companies have not disclosed specific emission reductions or cost savings for the Swiss market. The latest development expands the availability of container reuse within ONE’s logistics network. The carrier and Avantida have previously collaborated on similar services in other markets. Therefore, the Swiss introduction represents a geographical expansion of their existing cooperation rather than a new global partnership. ONE has not announced specific container volumes, participating locations or an implementation timetable for the Swiss service.

articles.title: SCHOTTEL Unveils New Thruster for Submarines and Underwater Vehicles
articles.summary: German propulsion specialist SCHOTTEL has introduced a new submersible auxiliary thruster designed to improve maneuverability and positioning accuracy for crewed and uncrewed underwater vehicles, including submarines.The SCHOTTEL PumpJet Submersible…
articles.body: SCHOTTEL Unveils New Thruster for Submarines and Underwater Vehicles Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 2, 2026 SCHOTTEL PumpJet Submersible SPJ-S (Credit: SCHOTTEL) German propulsion specialist SCHOTTEL has introduced a new submersible auxiliary thruster designed to improve maneuverability and positioning accuracy for crewed and uncrewed underwater vehicles, including submarines. The SCHOTTEL PumpJet Submersible SPJ-S provides continuously adjustable thrust through 360 degrees and is designed for civil and military underwater operations, including deepwater missions and maneuvering in confined spaces. The electrically driven system uses an impeller without a gearbox, enabling low-noise operation, while a pressure compensation system equalizes hydrostatic pressure at the seals to support operations at greater depths. Unlike retractable auxiliary propulsion systems, the SPJ-S provides immediate thrust without requiring deployment before use. The thruster is installed flush with the hull to avoid additional hydrodynamic resistance and reduce the risk of damage from seabed contact. Its construction also enables controlled bottoming on the seabed. The compact system can be integrated into platforms ranging from extra-large unmanned underwater vehicles (XLUUVs) to submarines. In addition to providing auxiliary propulsion, the SPJ-S can serve as a take-home propulsion system to maintain maneuverability in the event of main propulsion failure. The thruster is available in three sizes, covering a power range of approximately 50 to 990 kW. SCHOTTEL will present the SPJ-S for the first time at Euronaval 2026, taking place in Paris from November 3 to 6.

articles.summary: The UAE will protect its energy infrastructure and invest in new export routes, storage capacity abroad and shipping fleets to be better prepared for the US-Israeli war on Iran, its energy minister said on Monday.

REUTERS/Amr Alfiky ABU DHABI, Nov 2 (Reuters) – The UAE will protect its energy infrastructure and invest in new export routes, storage capacity abroad and shipping fleets to be better prepared for the US-Israeli war on Iran, its energy minister said on Monday. Minister Suhail al-Mazrouei said the course of the war could not be predicted, but the UAE would be more prepared than before. The UAE has been exporting crude via Fujairah, which sits just outside the Strait of Hormuz. It is building a new pipeline to Fujairah that will double crude capacity by next year. “I think after this crisis, many companies are going to look, think again, and design, redesign their facilities to be more resilient in the future,” Mazrouei told reporters on the sidelines of the Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition and Conference. “Resilience is a big word. And it has layers, from the barrel that you produce to the destination that you take it,” he said, adding: “You need to be closer to your customers.” Mazrouei earlier told the conference that at certain times his country’s exports were higher than prior to the war. Reuters had reported in June that the UAE boosted crude oil and condensate exports to a record high , shortly after it left the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries. articles.body: Europe Offshore OMV Petrom chief to exit as Neptun Deep nears first gas Bojan Lepic November 2, 2026 0 460 1 minute read OMV Petrom OMV Petrom Romanian oil and gas producer OMV Petrom is preparing for a leadership change as chief executive Christina Verchere has announced she will not seek another term, with her departure set to occur around the planned startup of the company’s flagship Neptun Deep gas development in the Black Sea. Verchere, who has led the company since May 2018, told supervisory board chair Emma Delaney she will not be available for another mandate after her current term expires on April 16, 2027. The company has not named a successor or disclosed the reasons behind her decision. “It has been a privilege for me to lead OMV Petrom for these past 9 years,” Verchere said, adding that she remained committed to delivering the company’s strategic projects during her remaining time in office. Her departure comes as OMV Petrom moves towards first gas from the €4bn ($4.48bn) Neptun Deep development, one of the largest offshore energy projects in the Black Sea. The company and its 50:50 partner Romgaz expect production to begin in the first half of 2027, with plateau output of around 8bn cubic metres annually targeted by the end of the third quarter. The development, located around 160 km offshore Romania, holds estimated recoverable resources of approximately 100bn cubic metres of gas. OMV Petrom’s latest quarterly update showed that eight of the ten planned development wells were completed, along with the installation of the Neptun Alpha production platform and the gas export pipeline to shore. The project was sanctioned in 2023 during Verchere’s tenure and is expected to transform Romania into a major regional gas supplier. Before joining OMV Petrom, Verchere spent more than two decades at BP, holding senior positions including regional president for Canada and Asia Pacific. articles.title: Nakilat Names Nine New Gas Carriers in South Korea

articles.body: Nakilat Names Nine New Gas Carriers in South Korea Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 2, 2026 (Credit Nakilat) Qatar Gas Transport Company (Nakilat) has named nine new gas carriers at three South Korean shipyards, marking progress in its fleet expansion programs aimed at increasing LNG transportation capacity and diversifying into LPG/ammonia shipping. The naming ceremonies, announced on November 2, took place at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, Hanwha Ocean and HD Hyundai Samho, covering seven LNG carriers and two LPG/ammonia carriers. Five of the LNG carriers form part of Nakilat's 25-vessel conventional-size LNG carrier newbuild program at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries and Hanwha Ocean. The 25 vessels will be fully owned and operated by Nakilat and chartered to QatarEnergy affiliates under long-term agreements, supporting LNG transportation requirements associated with Qatar's North Field expansion projects. The other four vessels, comprising two LNG carriers and two LPG/ammonia carriers, belong to Nakilat's separate six-vessel newbuild program at HD Hyundai Samho. The seven LNG carriers were named Al Ghuwair, Al Jazi, Al Mirzam, Maqdeem, Al Nasraniya, Energy Vigour and Energy Voyager, while the two LPG/ammonia carriers were named Energy South and Energy East. “We are proud of our partnership with QatarEnergy, through which we aim to deliver added value to the LNG transportation market as an active partner in meeting the requirements of the North Field expansion projects. “The naming of these nine vessels represents tangible progress in Nakilat’s long-term investment in expanding its fleet. By strengthening our LNG transportation capabilities and further diversifying our fleet with LPG/ammonia carriers, we are enhancing our ability to respond to our customers’ evolving needs while continuing to support Qatar’s position as one of the world’s leading producers and exporters of LNG,” said Abdullah Al Sulaiti, Chief Executive Officer of Nakilat The LNG newbuilds will support gas transportation from Qatar to international markets, while the LPG/ammonia carriers will expand Nakilat's range of shipping services. Nakilat operates a fleet comprising LNG and LPG carriers as well as a floating storage regasification unit (FSRU).

articles.title: PortXchange Expands Emissions Platform with Forecasting, AI Tools
articles.summary: Dutch maritime technology company PortXchange is expanding its EmissionInsider platform with emissions forecasting, scenario modelling and AI-assisted decarbonization planning tools to help ports assess the environmental impact of their operations…
articles.body: PortXchange Expands Emissions Platform with Forecasting, AI Tools Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 2, 2026 Sjoerd De Jager, Managing Director of PortXchange (Credit: PortXchange) Dutch maritime technology company PortXchange is expanding its EmissionInsider platform with emissions forecasting, scenario modelling and AI-assisted decarbonization planning tools to help ports assess the environmental impact of their operations and future investments. The planned upgrade will also introduce multimodal emissions monitoring, bringing together emissions data from vessels, trucks, rail movements and cargo-handling equipment, the company said. The expanded platform will comprise four connected products: Emission Report, Emission Dashboard, Emission Simulations and Emission Strategy. Emission Report will provide structured reporting for ports with different levels of data availability, while Emission Dashboard will support regular monitoring of port activity and emissions performance. The forecasting capabilities are being developed to help ports anticipate short-term emissions changes caused by factors such as weather disruptions, vessel schedule changes and increased waiting times at berths or anchorages. Emission Simulations will allow ports to assess the potential impact of investments and operational changes, including shore power installation, port equipment electrification, vessel speed limits and increased traffic volumes. The Emission Strategy product will introduce AI-assisted support for developing and reviewing decarbonisation plans, helping ports identify measures and priorities based on their operations, emissions profiles and objectives. “Ports have become much better at measuring emissions, but measuring them doesn’t make them disappear. “If the information sits in a report that nobody uses when making operational or investment decisions, we have to question what we’re achieving. Ports need to know where they can make a difference, what it will cost and whether their plans will actually reduce emissions,” said Sjoerd de Jager, Managing Director and Co-Founder of PortXchange. PortXchange plans to introduce the new capabilities progressively, with a modular structure allowing ports to select products and data integrations according to their operational and decarbonisation requirements.

articles.body: Exploration & Production November 2, 2026 · 1 minute ago Gas flows from Southeast Asian offshore field 21 months after FID Eni and Petronas’ Searah has brought online an Asian gas field, flowing 250 million standard cubic feet per day (scfd) to domestic and export markets. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email FPU Jangkrik Source: Eni Searah, a joint venture (JV) between Italy’s Eni and Malaysia’s Petronas, has achieved first gas from the Maha gas field in the Kutei Basin just 21 months after its final investment decision (FID), boosting regional energy security and liquefied natural gas (LNG) capacity. Eni has announced the start-up of gas production from the Maha field in the West Ganal block at Indonesia’s Kutei Basin at a water depth of approximately 1,000 meters. This field comprises two subsea production wells connected to the existing Jangkrik floating production unit (FPU) by approximately 12 kilometers of flowlines. Following initial processing onboard the FPU, the gas will be transported through the pipeline network to supply the domestic market and the Bontang liquefaction plant, which supplies LNG to both domestic and export markets. The Maha field can produce 250 million standard cubic feet per day, bringing combined production from the Jangkrik FPU and the South Hub to a plateau of 750 million scfd. The Gendalo and Gendang project’s expected start-up and tie-in to the same FPU in 2028 will extend this plateau beyond the end of the decade. According to Eni, the execution and start-up of production at Maha, following the start-up of Merakes East in May 2025, together with the final investment decisions announced in March 2026 for the North Hub ( Geng North and Gehem ) and South Hub (Gendalo and Gendang) projects, underscore its broader strategy to efficiently develop the gas resources discovered in Indonesia’s Kutei Basin. Fortius Offshore Wind and Fram Wind Solutions have been selected to receive support for projects at the METCentre offshore wind demonstration facility in Rogaland. The awards follow a competitive funding process that attracted five applications. Fortius, owned by Deep Wind Offshore, has been allocated NOK2bn, while Fram Wind Solutions, backed by BW Offshore and Grieg Kapital, will receive NOK1.94bn. Both developers plan to install their turbines within the next five years, with funding to be paid out subject to the projects being realised. The projects will test floating foundations capable of supporting large turbines, mooring systems and new approaches to offshore construction, installation and operation. Enova assessed the proposals against criteria including expected electricity generation per krone of funding, technology scalability, environmental impact and potential future cost reductions. The developers signed a joint development agreement in July to use existing infrastructure associated with the retired Taean coal-fired power station, potentially reducing grid connection costs. articles.body: Interconnectors November 2, 2026 · 1 minute ago UK's 2 GW subsea power cable gets government's approval NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email National Grid The UK government has granted development consent for the 2 GW Sea Link subsea high-voltage direct current (HVDC) electricity connection between Kent and Suffolk. Sea Link is expected to enter construction in early 2027 and is one of the key infrastructure projects of the National Grid Electricity Transmission's (NGET) Great Grid Upgrade, which aims to substantially increase electricity transmission capacity in the UK. The 2 GW project will have converter stations in Suffolk and Kent, linked by a 140-kilometer 525 kV subsea cable through the North Sea and Thames Estuary. The project will be capable of carrying enough electricity to power the equivalent of 2 million homes. "Britain’s future rests on rebuilding the national grid so renewable energy and businesses can connect, driving economic growth and reducing our exposure to volatile global fossil fuel markets which are driving up all our bills," said the UK's Energy Minister Michael Shanks . "By rewiring Britain we get homegrown power to where it’s needed, we make sure the grid is resilient for the future and we bring bills down for good." Furthermore, the UK government community benefits scheme will be delivered by National Grid with over £1 million (around €1.2 million) each for community funds in Kent and Suffolk. At the end of 2025, Japanese Sumitomo Electric Industries was contracted to supply and install 140 kilometers of subsea cable for the electricity connection. The 525 kV HVDC cable will be produced at the company's submarine cable factory at Port of Nigg in Scotland. articles.body: Asia Greater China Shipyards Tankers Yangzijiang Maritime extends tanker buying spree at Haifeng Adis Ajdin November 2, 2026 0 855 1 minute read Yangzijiang Financial Yangzijiang Financial Singapore-listed Yangzijiang Maritime Development has signed a contract for four 50,000 dwt MR product tankers at Jiangsu Haifeng Shipbuilding, extending its extensive newbuilding programme in China. The Ren Yuanlin-led group recently concluded the deal after several rounds of tanker orders at Haifeng this year. No contract price or delivery schedule has been disclosed. The two companies began working together in January with contracts covering two firm plus six optional MR tankers and two firm plus two optional LR2s. Another four MRs and two LR2s followed in August, before Yangzijiang returned at the end of September for six firm 114,000 dwt LR2 tankers with two options. The latest agreement has been described as a further four-ship contract, although it remains unclear whether any of the vessels represent the conversion of previously agreed options. Yangzijiang has pursued an aggressive strategy of booking newbuildings at smaller Chinese yards and subsequently monetising the assets through sales, charters and financing arrangements. Last week, the company disclosed agreements to sell another six MR tanker newbuildings for $308m, lifting contracted vessel resales to 18 ships worth $805m over ten months. The latest disposals included two 49,500 dwt tankers scheduled for completion in 2026 and 2027 and four 49,800 dwt units due in 2027 and 2028.
